title: Definitions & Fei-Fei Li functional taxonomy
summary: "World model" is the most overloaded term in AI: computer vision, robotics, RL, and generative AI each claim to build one and each means something different (worldlabs.ai/blog/taxonomy-of-world-models). The concept traces to Kenneth Craik (1943), who argued minds run "small-scale models" of reality. Three reference definitions anchor the debate. (1) Ha & Schmidhuber (2018, arXiv 1803.10122): a world model is an unsupervised generative neural net that learns a "compressed spatial and temporal representation" of an RL environment; their V (VAE) + M (MDN-RNN) + C (linear controller, trained via CMA-ES) agent can train "entirely inside of its own hallucinated dream" and transfer back. This lineage continues in Hafner's Dreamer/DreamerV3 (arXiv 2301.04104), which learns a latent RSSM world model and trains actor-critic on imagined rollouts, first to mine diamonds in Minecraft from scratch. (2) LeCun's "A Path Towards Autonomous Machine Intelligence" (2022) makes the world model one of six modules (configurator, perception, world model, cost, actor, short-term memory). His JEPA / Hierarchical-JEPA is explicitly "a non-generative architecture for predictive world models" that predicts in abstract representation space (not pixels), handles uncertainty via latent variables, and enables hierarchical planning — he bets against pixel-reconstruction/generative approaches (cis.temple.edu PDF; ai.meta.com). (3) Fei-Fei Li / World Labs reframes world models as the substrate of "spatial intelligence" — "a new type of generative model" that is generative, multimodal, and interactive, going beyond LLMs that remain "wordsmiths in the dark" (drfeifei.substack.com, Nov 10 2025). The SEED ARTICLE, "A Functional Taxonomy of World Models" (Fei-Fei Li + World Labs team, June 3 2026), grounds everything in the POMDP loop (agent→action→state→observation) and splits world models by OUTPUT into three functional types: Renderers (output pixels for human eyes; Genie 3, RTFM, Nano Banana), Simulators (output geometrically/physically/dynamically faithful STATE; Marble, NVIDIA Omniverse), and Planners (output actions given observation+goal; VLA models, World Action Models). Simulators are the "linchpin/bridge" since "geometry, physics, and dynamics are the world itself"; the three types are "three projections of a single underlying understanding." Industry instances: DeepMind Genie 3 (720p, 24fps, ~1 min consistency, real-time, "stepping stone on the path to AGI," Aug 5 2025).

keyClaims.claim: "World model" is one of the most overloaded terms in AI: computer vision, robotics, reinforcement learning, and generative AI each claim to build world models and each means something quite different.

The seed article 'A Functional Taxonomy of World Models' (subtitle: 'Renderers, Simulators, Planners, and the Loop That Connects Them') was published June 3, 2026 by Dr. Fei-Fei Li with the World Labs team, and frames world models via the POMDP agent-environment loop: an agent takes actions that affect the world's state, but the agent never sees state directly, only partial observations.

The seed article's taxonomy distinguishes three functional categories by what they OUTPUT. RENDERER: 'outputs observations in the form of pixels meant for human eyes, and the quality that matters most is visual fidelity' (takes actions in, produces observations).

SIMULATOR (seed article): 'outputs state: a geometrically, physically or dynamically faithful representation of the world that humans and computer programs can both compute on and interact with.' Simulators demand accuracy beyond visual plausibility (geometry that holds under inspection, physics respecting Newton's laws).

PLANNER (seed article): 'outputs actions. Given an observation and a goal, a planner answers the question of what the agent should do next.' The category includes Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models and World Action Models.

Named examples per category in the seed article: Renderers = Google Genie 3, World Labs RTFM, Google Nano Banana; Simulators = World Labs Marble, NVIDIA Omniverse; Planners = Vision-Language-Action models and World Action Models.

The seed article argues the three categories are unified: a model that truly understands how a cup sits on a table 'should be able to render that cup from any angle, simulate what happens when the cup is pushed, and plan for a hand to pick the cup up. The three categories are three projections of a single underlying understanding.' Simulators are the 'bridge' and 'linchpin' because geometry, physics, and dynamics 'are the world itself.'

The seed article critiques renderers as optimizing visual plausibility over physical accuracy: a renderer can be beautiful but 'cannot be trusted to design a building or train a robot' (e.g. video models producing physically impossible flames), whereas simulators serve both human eyes and computational agents like robots and RL systems.

Ha & Schmidhuber 'World Models' (arXiv:1803.10122, March 2018) define a world model as a generative neural network trained unsupervised to 'learn a compressed spatial and temporal representation of the environment,' and show an agent 'can even train entirely inside of its own hallucinated dream generated by its world model, and transfer this policy back into the actual environment.'

The Ha/Schmidhuber architecture has three components: Vision (V) = a VAE compressing frames to a latent vector; Memory (M) = a Mixture-Density Network RNN (MDN-RNN) predicting the next latent given past latents and actions; Controller (C) = a small linear policy over the latent and RNN hidden state, optimized with CMA-ES. Tested on CarRacing and VizDoom.

Yann LeCun's 'A Path Towards Autonomous Machine Intelligence' (2022 position paper) proposes a cognitive architecture of six modules: Configurator (goal/control), Perception, World Model, Cost, Actor, and Short-term Memory; all modules are differentiable and many trainable.

LeCun's world model is realized via JEPA / Hierarchical-JEPA, described as 'a non-generative architecture for predictive world models that learn a hierarchy of representations.' It predicts in an abstract embedding space rather than reconstructing pixels, uses latent variables to capture multiple plausible futures, and serves as 'the basis of predictive world models for hierarchical planning under uncertainty.' LeCun explicitly bets against generative/reconstruction approaches.

Fei-Fei Li's essay 'From Words to Worlds: Spatial Intelligence is AI's Next Frontier' (November 10, 2025) defines world models as 'a new type of generative models whose capabilities of understanding, reasoning, generation and interaction with the semantically, physically, geometrically and dynamically complex worlds...are far beyond the reach of today's LLMs,' which 'remain wordsmiths in the dark; eloquent but inexperienced, knowledgeable but ungrounded.'

Fei-Fei Li lists three essential capabilities a world model must have: Generative (generate worlds with perceptual, geometric, and physical consistency), Multimodal (handle images, videos, depth maps, text, gestures, or actions as input), and Interactive (output the next state based on input actions). World Labs co-founders: Justin Johnson, Christoph Lassner, Ben Mildenhall, and Fei-Fei Li.

World Labs' Marble is described as the first world model promptable by multimodal inputs to generate and maintain consistent 3D environments; RTFM (Real-Time Frame Model) is a real-time generative frame-based model using spatially-grounded frames.

Google DeepMind defines world models as 'AI systems that can use their understanding of the world to simulate aspects of it, enabling agents to predict both how an environment will evolve and how their actions will affect it,' and calls them 'a key stepping stone on the path to AGI.'

Genie 3 (announced August 5, 2025) is a general-purpose world model that generates dynamic interactive environments in real time from a text prompt at 720p / 24fps, with consistency 'for several minutes' and visual memory extending ~one minute back; it generates frames auto-regressively, supports 'promptable world events,' and was tested with DeepMind's SIMA embodied agent. It is the first Genie model to allow real-time interaction, improving on Genie 2.

DreamerV3 (Hafner et al., 'Mastering Diverse Domains through World Models,' arXiv:2301.04104) learns a latent world model (Recurrent State-Space Model) and trains an actor-critic purely on imagined rollouts in latent space; it was the first agent to collect diamonds in Minecraft from scratch with no human data, and reaches SOTA across DeepMind Control, Atari, and Minecraft with fixed hyperparameters.

Academically, the definition debate splits along two axes: 'understanding the world' (building internal representations of mechanisms, the Ha/Schmidhuber lineage) vs 'predicting the future' (simulating future states to guide decisions, the LeCun emphasis); a comprehensive survey ('Understanding World or Predicting Future?', arXiv:2411.14499) frames world models as internal simulators capturing environment dynamics for forward and counterfactual rollouts.

The core consensus definition (Wikipedia): 'A world model in artificial intelligence is a machine learning system that builds an internal representation of an environment [and] predicts how that environment changes over time in response to actions,' with three conceptual variants: internal/latent representations, predictive systems (encoder+predictor), and generative/interactive models that output consistent video or 3D scenes.

The 'world model' concept originates with Kenneth Craik's 1943 work, in which the mind runs a 'small-scale model' of external reality; the seed article traces the term to Craik (1943) and its formalization via the POMDP framework in reinforcement learning.

openQuestions: Whether the seed article's output-based taxonomy (Renderer/Simulator/Planner) and the academic understand-vs-predict axis are reconcilable, or describe orthogonal cuts of the same space.

Whether a single model can simultaneously be a faithful Simulator (physically accurate state) and a high-fidelity Renderer (photoreal pixels), or whether the fidelity-vs-plausibility tradeoff forces specialization.

Whether LeCun's non-generative JEPA bet (predict in abstract space) or the generative/interactive video-and-3D approach (Genie, Marble, Sora-style) will prove the more scalable substrate for world models.

How to empirically measure 'physical/geometric/dynamic faithfulness' of a simulator versus mere visual plausibility — the seed article asserts the distinction but standardized benchmarks are unsettled.
Whether 'spatial intelligence' (Fei-Fei Li) is a distinct capability requiring 3D-native world models, or whether sufficiently scaled video/multimodal models acquire it implicitly.

The precise boundary between a 'world model' and an 'agent/planner': LeCun and the seed article treat the planner as separate from the world model, whereas Ha/Schmidhuber and Dreamer fold prediction and control into one system.

title: Foundational architectures
summary: "Foundational architectures" for world models trace to Schmidhuber's early-1990s RNN "world model + controller" (C-M) framework ("Making the World Differentiable," FKI-126-90, TUM 1990), where one RNN learns to predict the environment and a second controller acts inside it. Ha & Schmidhuber's "World Models" (arXiv:1803.10122, Mar 2018; NeurIPS 2018 version "Recurrent World Models Facilitate Policy Evolution," arXiv:1809.01999) operationalized this with three explicitly separated modules: V (a VAE compressing each 64x64x3 frame into a latent z; dim 32 for CarRacing, 64 for VizDoom), M (an MDN-RNN/LSTM that models the density P(z_{t+1} | a_t, z_t, h_t) as a mixture of 5 diagonal Gaussians; 256 LSTM units for CarRacing, 512 for VizDoom; a recurrent version of Bishop's 1995 mixture-density network, lineage from Graves' handwriting RNN), and C (a tiny linear controller a_t = W_c[z_t h_t] + b_c with only 867 / 1088 parameters, trained by CMA-ES, population 64). On CarRacing-v0 it scored 906±21 over 100 trials (solving threshold 900), beating prior DQN/A3C baselines (343-652) and the leaderboard best (838±11). On VizDoom Take Cover, the controller was trained *entirely inside the dream* (M used as a simulator predicting z and done), transferring to ~1100 real timesteps; the temperature tau (e.g. tau=1.15) controls dream stochasticity and prevents the controller from exploiting the model's adversarial flaws — at tau=0.1 it scored 2086 in-dream but only 193 in reality. PlaNet (Hafner et al., arXiv:1811.04551, 2018/ICLR'19, Google Brain/DeepMind) introduced the Recurrent State Space Model (RSSM), splitting latent state into a deterministic GRU path h_t = f(h_{t-1}, s_{t-1}, a_{t-1}) and a stochastic path p(s_t|h_t), with observation p(o_t|h_t,s_t), reward p(r_t|h_t,s_t) and posterior q(s_t|h_t,o_t) — "a non-linear Kalman filter / sequential VAE." Ablations showed both paths are essential. PlaNet plans online with CEM-MPC (horizon 12, 1000 candidates, 10 iters, top-100 refit), matching D4PG with ~50x less data. Dreamer (arXiv:1912.01603, ICLR 2020) reused the RSSM but replaced planning with "latent imagination": it learns an actor q(a|s) and value v(s) by backpropagating analytic gradients of lambda-returns through imagined latent rollouts (horizon 15), reaching 823 average on 20 DMC tasks at 5e6 steps, 3 h/1e6 steps vs PlaNet's 11 h.

keyClaims.claim: Ha & Schmidhuber's World Models (2018) agent has three explicitly separated components: V (Vision, a VAE compressing observations into latent z), M (Memory, an MDN-RNN predicting the future), and C (a small linear Controller mapping [z_t, h_t] to actions).

The V model is a Variational Autoencoder that encodes each 64x64x3 RGB frame into a latent vector z of dimension 32 (CarRacing) or 64 (VizDoom), using 4 stride-2 conv layers to mu_t and sigma_t and 4 deconv layers to reconstruct; trained 1 epoch with L2 reconstruction + KL loss.

The M model is an MDN-RNN (LSTM + Mixture Density Network) that models the probability density P(z_{t+1} | a_t, z_t, h_t) as a mixture of 5 diagonal-covariance Gaussians; the LSTM has 256 hidden units for CarRacing and 512 for VizDoom. It is a recurrent version of Bishop's (1995) mixture-of-Gaussians network outputting softmax mixture weights, linear means, and variances.

The C model (controller) is a single linear layer a_t = W_c [z_t h_t] + b_c with a tanh nonlinearity, having only 867 parameters (CarRacing) or 1088 (VizDoom); it is deliberately tiny so it can be optimized by CMA-ES (population size 64, each candidate evaluated over 16 rollouts), which works well for solution spaces of a few thousand parameters.

Component parameter counts: V model ~4.35M (CarRacing) / ~4.45M (VizDoom); M model 422,368 (CarRacing) / 1,678,785 (VizDoom); C model 867 / 1088 — illustrating the deliberate asymmetry where almost all capacity is in the world model and almost none in the policy.

On CarRacing-v0, the World Models agent achieved 906 +/- 21 over 100 random trials, exceeding the 900-over-100-trials solving threshold and setting a new state of the art; prior Deep RL baselines scored DQN 343+/-18, A3C-continuous 591+/-45, A3C-discrete 652+/-10, and the previous leaderboard best 838+/-11.

For VizDoom Take Cover, the controller was trained entirely inside the 'dream' (the M model used as a simulator predicting both z_{t+1} and the done/terminal flag), never touching the game engine during policy optimization, and the dream-trained policy transferred to ~1100 real-environment timesteps (vs the 750 needed to 'solve').

The MDN-RNN temperature parameter tau controls dream stochasticity and prevents the controller from exploiting adversarial imperfections of the world model: at tau=0.10 the agent scored 2086+/-140 in the dream but only 193+/-58 in reality, whereas tau=1.15 gave 918+/-546 in-dream and the best real transfer of 1092+/-556. Higher tau makes the dream harder/noisier and closes the reality gap.

The World Models lineage combines concepts from Schmidhuber's 1990-2015 work on RNN-based world models and controllers, including 'Making the World Differentiable' (FKI-126-90, TUM, 1990), which proposed using a fully recurrent self-supervised network as a differentiable model of the environment that a controller can plan within, plus curiosity/intrinsic motivation (1990-91) and 'Learning to Think' (2015).

PlaNet (Hafner et al., arXiv:1811.04551, Google Brain/DeepMind, 2018/ICLR 2019) is a purely model-based agent that learns dynamics from pixels and plans in latent space; its core is the Recurrent State Space Model (RSSM) with a 30-dimensional latent state.

The RSSM splits the latent state into a deterministic recurrent path h_t = f(h_{t-1}, s_{t-1}, a_{t-1}) (implemented as a GRU with 200 units) and a stochastic path with prior p(s_t|h_t), plus an observation model p(o_t|h_t,s_t), reward model p(r_t|h_t,s_t), and posterior/encoder q(s_t|h_t,o_t); the authors describe it as a non-linear Kalman filter or sequential VAE.

PlaNet ablations show both paths are necessary: a purely deterministic RNN cannot represent multiple plausible futures, and a purely stochastic SSM cannot reliably retain information over many timesteps ('the agent does not learn without' the deterministic component); only the combined RSSM solves all tasks.

PlaNet introduced 'latent overshooting,' a training objective that generalizes the one-step variational ELBO to enforce consistency of multi-step (distance d) latent predictions p_d via KL terms, improving long-horizon accuracy without decoding images at every step.

PlaNet plans online with the Cross Entropy Method (CEM) for Model Predictive Control: planning horizon H=12, J=1000 candidate action sequences per iteration, top K=100 refit, I=10 iterations, evaluating rewards purely in latent space (no image generation during planning).

PlaNet matches or beats model-free baselines with far less data: it outperforms A3C (trained from states for 100,000 episodes) and reaches D4PG-level performance using roughly one-fiftieth the episodes, on six DeepMind Control Suite tasks (cartpole swingup, finger spin, cheetah run, cup catch, walker walk, etc.) from 64x64x3 pixels, training in 10-20 h on one Nvidia V100.

Dreamer (Hafner, Lillicrap, Ba, Norouzi; arXiv:1912.01603, ICLR 2020) reuses PlaNet's RSSM world model but replaces online CEM planning with 'latent imagination': it learns a parametric actor q_phi(a|s) and value v_psi(s) by backpropagating analytic gradients of multi-step lambda-returns through the learned latent dynamics over an imagination horizon H=15.

Dreamer's value target is a lambda-weighted return V_lambda mixing n-step returns, and behavior learning maximizes the expected sum of these values over imagined trajectories; the transition model predicts ahead in compact latent space, enabling thousands of parallel imagined rollouts without rendering images.

Dreamer reached 823 average score across 20 DeepMind Control Suite tasks within 5x10^6 environment steps, exceeding model-free D4PG (786 at 1x10^8 steps) and PlaNet (332 at 5x10^6 steps), while training at ~3 hours per 1e6 steps vs PlaNet's 11 hours and D4PG's 24 hours.

The key conceptual distinction across the lineage: Ha & Schmidhuber train a tiny linear controller by evolution inside MDN-RNN dreams; PlaNet does derivative-free online planning (CEM) each step with no learned policy; Dreamer learns an actor-critic by differentiating value estimates through the RSSM dynamics — three different ways to use a learned latent world model for control.

openQuestions: How much do the World Models results depend on training M (the MDN-RNN) at all? Tallec et al.'s reproduction (ctallec.github.io/world-models) questioned whether training the recurrent model is necessary or whether a random RNN feature extractor suffices for CarRacing.
The reality gap when training purely in the dream: temperature tuning (tau~1.15) was needed for VizDoom transfer, but it remains task-specific and hand-tuned rather than principled.

PlaNet's RSSM uses a single 30-dim Gaussian latent; later work (DreamerV2/V3) moved to categorical/discrete latents — open question of why continuous Gaussian latents underperform discrete ones for world modeling.

Scaling of the V+M+C decomposition: the linear CMA-ES controller works only because the world model does the heavy lifting, but it does not obviously scale to high-dimensional action spaces or long-horizon credit assignment.

Whether explicit reconstruction (decoding pixels in V/observation model) is needed at all, or whether reward/value-only or contrastive latent objectives can replace it without losing dynamics fidelity.

verifiedClaims.claim: Ha & Schmidhuber's World Models (2018) agent has three explicitly separated components: V (Vision, a VAE compressing observations into latent z), M (Memory, an MDN-RNN predicting the future), and C (a small linear Controller mapping [z_t, h_t] to actions).
verifiedClaims.evidence: Every architectural detail is confirmed verbatim by the authors' canonical primary source, worldmodels.github.io. (1) Three separated components: "Our agent consists of three components that work closely together: Vision (V), Memory (M), and Controller (C)." (2) V = VAE: "We use a Variational Autoencoder (VAE) as the V model," which "compresses each frame it receives at time step t into a low dimensional latent vector z." (3) M = MDN-RNN predicting the future: "a Mixture Density Network combined with a RNN (MDN-RNN)" that outputs "the probability distribution of the next latent vector z_(t+1)," i.e. P(z_(t+1) | a_t, z_t, h_t). (4) C = small linear controller on [z_t, h_t]: "C is a simple single layer linear model that maps z_t and h_t directly to action a_t at each time step," with equation a_t = W_c [z_t h_t] + b_c; the design is deliberately small so "most of our agent's complexity resides in the world model (V and M)." Independently corroborated by the ctallec PyTorch reimplementation README, which describes "a linear Controller (C), which takes both the latent encoding of the current frame, and the hidden state of the MDN-RNN... as input and outputs an action." CAVEAT on the cited sources (not the substance): the two URLs are genuine Ha & Schmidhuber primary sources but are different documents. The paper literally titled "World Models" is arXiv 1803.10122; the cited arXiv 1809.01999 is the companion NeurIPS 2018 version titled "Recurrent World Models Facilitate Policy Evolution" (same authors, same architecture, different title). So the architecture claim is accurate, though the "1809.01999 = World Models" label is slightly mismatched. arXiv PDFs were image-based and did not extract as text via fetch, so the verbatim quotes rely on the github.io companion site plus the independent reimplementation README.

verifiedClaims.evidence: Every specific, falsifiable detail is confirmed verbatim by the primary source (Ha & Schmidhuber, "World Models," arXiv:1803.10122, Appendix A.1), cross-checked against the canonical interactive article at worldmodels.github.io. I extracted the appendix text directly from the arXiv PDF. Quoted verbatim: "We trained a Convolutional Variational Autoencoder (ConvVAE) model as the V Model"; "we first resize each image to 64x64 pixels... three floating point values between 0 and 1 to represent each of the RGB channels. The ConvVAE takes in this 64x64x3 input tensor and passes this data through 4 convolutional layers to encode it into low dimension vectors mu and sigma, each of size Nz"; "In the Car Racing task, Nz is 32 while for the Doom task Nz is 64"; "The latent vector z is passed through 4 of deconvolution layers used to decode and reconstruct the image"; "Each convolution and deconvolution layer uses a stride of 2"; "We trained the model for 1 epoch over the data collected from a random policy, using L2 distance between the input image and the reconstruction to quantify the reconstruction loss we optimize for, in addition to KL loss." All seven claim components (VAE; 64x64x3 RGB input; Nz=32 CarRacing / Nz=64 Doom/VizDoom; 4 conv layers producing mu and sigma; 4 deconv layers; stride 2; 1 epoch; L2 + KL loss) match exactly, with no contradictions found. Minor notational nuance: the appendix writes the Gaussian params as "mu, sigma" without the t-subscript, but the paper's main body uses the time-subscripted form N(mu_t, sigma_t^2 I), so "mu_t/sigma_t" in the claim is also faithful to the source. The claim's "VizDoom" maps to the paper's "Doom"/"DoomTakeCover (ViZDoom: Take Cover)" task -- same environment.

title: Dreamer line & model-based RL in imagination
summary: The "Dreamer" line (Danijar Hafner et al.) established model-based RL that learns behaviors purely inside a learned latent world model ("imagination"), eliminating online environment interaction during policy optimization. DreamerV1 ("Dream to Control," Dec 2019, ICLR 2020) used a PlaNet-derived Recurrent State-Space Model (RSSM) with Gaussian latents and trained an actor (action model) + critic (value model) entirely in latent rollouts (horizon H=15, lambda-returns) by backpropagating ANALYTIC value gradients through imagined trajectories — its core novelty vs Reinforce. DreamerV2 ("Mastering Atari with Discrete World Models," Oct 2020, ICLR 2021) switched the RSSM stochastic state to 32 categorical variables x 32 classes (straight-through gradients) plus KL balancing (alpha=0.8), and was the first agent to reach human-level on Atari-55 by learning only in its world model (gamer-normalized median 2.15, beating Rainbow 1.47 and IQN 1.29 at 200M frames, ~10 days on one V100). DreamerV3 (arXiv Jan 2023; Nature, 2 Apr 2025) is a SINGLE fixed-hyperparameter algorithm spanning 150+ tasks across 8 domains, enabled by robustness tricks: symlog transforms, two-hot symexp reward/value encoding, free bits (1 nat) KL clipping, and percentile return normalization. It was the first to collect Minecraft diamonds from scratch (within 100M env steps, no human data/curricula) and shows clean scaling — larger models (12M-400M params) yield BOTH higher final scores and more data efficiency. DayDreamer (Jun 2022, CoRL 2022) deployed DreamerV2-style world models on 4 REAL robots with an async learner/actor on a single GPU, no simulator: a Unitree A1 learned to stand and walk in ~1 hour, UR5/XArm visual pick-and-place from sparse rewards (2.5-3.1 objects/min after 8-10h), and a Sphero navigated from pixels in 2h. TD-MPC (ICML 2022) and TD-MPC2 (ICLR 2024) are a parallel model-based line using a DECODER-FREE implicit latent world model trained by joint-embedding consistency (no reconstruction), combining short-horizon MPPI planning in latent space with a TD-learned terminal value; TD-MPC2 matches one config across 104 continuous-control tasks and trains a single 317M-param agent on 80 tasks, scaling 1M-317M params.

keyClaims.claim: DreamerV1 ('Dream to Control: Learning Behaviors by Latent Imagination', Hafner, Lillicrap, Ba, Norouzi) was posted to arXiv 3 Dec 2019 and published at ICLR 2020; it learns action and value models PURELY in latent imagination by propagating analytic gradients of value estimates back through trajectories imagined in the compact latent space of a learned world model.

DreamerV1's world model is a PlaNet-derived RSSM with ~30-dimensional diagonal-Gaussian latent states learned via image reconstruction; the actor (tanh-Gaussian policy) and critic (value) are trained over imagination horizon H=15 using lambda-returns (gamma=0.99, lambda=0.95), and the actor maximizes value by backpropagating analytic gradients through the learned dynamics rather than using Reinforce or derivative-free planning.

On 20 visual continuous-control tasks from the DeepMind Control Suite, DreamerV1 reached ~823 average score after ~5e6 environment steps, exceeding D4PG (786 at 1e8 steps) and PlaNet (332), and was far faster computationally (~3 hours per 1e6 steps vs 11h for PlaNet and 24h for D4PG).

DreamerV2 ('Mastering Atari with Discrete World Models', Hafner, Lillicrap, Norouzi, Ba) was posted to arXiv 5 Oct 2020 and published at ICLR 2021; it is the first agent to achieve human-level performance on the Atari benchmark of 55 tasks by learning behaviors purely from predictions inside a separately trained world model.

DreamerV2's key change is a discrete/categorical RSSM latent: 32 categorical variables each with 32 classes, optimized with straight-through gradients, plus KL balancing with alpha=0.8 (scaling prior cross-entropy vs posterior entropy differently). The actor and critic are trained in imagination over horizon H=15 with lambda-returns (lambda=0.95); for Atari the actor uses pure Reinforce gradients (rho=1) plus entropy regularization.

On Atari-55 at 200M frames, DreamerV2 reaches a gamer-normalized median score of 2.15, exceeding Rainbow (1.47) and IQN (1.29); it surpasses these top single-GPU agents using a single NVIDIA V100 GPU in under 10 days.

DreamerV3 ('Mastering Diverse Domains through World Models', Hafner, Pasukonis, Ba, Lillicrap) was posted to arXiv 10 Jan 2023 (v1); it outperforms specialized methods across over 150 diverse tasks with a SINGLE fixed configuration, including continuous/discrete actions, visual/low-dimensional inputs, 2D/3D worlds, and varying data budgets, reward frequencies and scales.

DreamerV3 was published in Nature on 2 April 2025 ('Mastering diverse control tasks through world models', Nature 640(8059):647-653) spanning 8 domains: Atari, ProcGen, DMLab, Atari100k, Proprio Control Suite, Visual Control Suite, BSuite, and others; it comprises a world model (RSSM), a critic, and an actor, where the actor and critic learn purely from abstract latent trajectories predicted by the world model over planning horizon T=16.

DreamerV3's cross-domain robustness comes from: symlog transformation symlog(x)=sign(x)ln(|x|+1) with inverse symexp; two-hot encoded distributional reward/value targets (K=255 buckets) in symexp space; free bits clipping KL losses below 1 nat; KL balancing; percentile return normalization (95th-5th percentile, clamped to min 1) so sparse near-zero rewards are not amplified; and a fixed entropy scale eta=3e-4 across all domains.

DreamerV3 is the first algorithm to collect diamonds in Minecraft from scratch without human data or curricula; all Dreamer agents discover diamonds within 100 million environment steps (first diamond after ~29-30M steps on average, roughly equivalent to ~17 days of in-game play), applied out of the box.

DreamerV3 exhibits clean scaling: parameter variants of 12M, 25M, 50M, 100M, 200M and 400M (the arXiv version reports an XS-XL family ~8M-200M), where larger models achieve both higher final scores AND require less interaction (greater data efficiency); it outperforms a well-tuned PPO across all domains while using fixed hyperparameters.

DreamerV3 benchmark numbers: Atari100k gamer-normalized 49% (vs IRIS 29%); Atari-200M median 302% (vs DreamerV2 219%); on DMLab it reaches 54.2% normalized at 50M steps vs IMPALA's 51.3% at 10B steps, a ~200x data-efficiency improvement.

DayDreamer ('World Models for Physical Robot Learning', Wu, Escontrela, Hafner, Goldberg, Abbeel) was posted to arXiv 28 Jun 2022 (CoRL 2022); it applies a DreamerV2-style world model + actor-critic learned in imagination to 4 real robots online with NO simulator, using an asynchronous actor process and learner process (learner samples the replay buffer) and the same hyperparameters across all experiments.

DayDreamer on a Unitree A1 quadruped: learns to roll off its back, stand up and walk from scratch without resets in only 1 hour (rotating/feet down by ~5 min, standing and walking by ~20 min), and adapts within ~10 minutes (~30 min mark) to withstand external pushes; a SAC baseline could only rotate and place feet, failing to stand or walk.

DayDreamer on two robotic arms learns multi-object pick-and-place directly from camera images and sparse rewards, approaching human performance: a UR5 reached ~2.5 objects/min after ~8 hours of training, and an XArm reached ~3.1 objects/min after ~10 hours; PPO and Rainbow baselines failed to learn due to sample inefficiency.

DayDreamer on a Sphero Ollie wheeled robot learns to navigate to a goal position purely from camera images (automatically resolving orientation ambiguity) in ~2 hours; a DrQv2 model-free baseline performed similarly on this comparatively easy task.

TD-MPC ('Temporal Difference Learning for Model Predictive Control', Hansen, Wang, Su, ICML 2022, arXiv 2203.04955) learns a Task-Oriented Latent Dynamics (TOLD) model plus a terminal value function jointly by TD learning, then at inference performs MPPI trajectory optimization over short-horizon latent rollouts using the value for long-term return; it solved high-dimensional Humanoid and Dog locomotion in 1M environment steps (first reported Dog result).

TD-MPC2 ('Scalable, Robust World Models for Continuous Control', Hansen, Su, Wang, ICLR 2024 Spotlight, arXiv 2310.16828, posted 25 Oct 2023) uses a DECODER-FREE implicit world model (encoder, latent dynamics, reward predictor, ensemble of 5 terminal Q-functions, and a max-entropy policy prior) trained by joint-embedding latent consistency (no reconstruction), with reward/value via discrete regression in log space and SimNorm simplex normalization; planning is MPPI in latent space bootstrapped by the learned terminal value.

TD-MPC2 compares favorably to model-free and model-based methods (SAC, DreamerV3 at ~20M params, and original TD-MPC) across 104 continuous-control tasks spanning 4 domains (DMControl 39, Meta-World 50, ManiSkill2 5, MyoSuite 10) with a single set of hyperparameters.

TD-MPC2 demonstrates multitask scaling: a single 317M-parameter agent performs 80 tasks (50 Meta-World + 30 DMControl) across multiple embodiments and action spaces, trained on 545M transitions from replay buffers of 240 single-task agents; capabilities increase consistently across 5 model sizes from 1M to 317M parameters (normalized score scales ~linearly with log(parameters)). The authors released 324 checkpoints and two datasets (545M/34GB and 345M/20GB transitions).

verifiedClaims.claim: DreamerV1 ('Dream to Control: Learning Behaviors by Latent Imagination', Hafner, Lillicrap, Ba, Norouzi) was posted to arXiv 3 Dec 2019, published at ICLR 2020, and learns action and value models purely in latent imagination by propagating analytic gradients of value estimates back through trajectories imagined in the compact latent space of a learned world model.
verifiedClaims.evidence: Every element of the claim is confirmed by primary sources. (1) Title and authors: The arXiv abstract page (1912.01603) and the ar5iv full text both give the exact title "Dream to Control: Learning Behaviors by Latent Imagination" and the author list Danijar Hafner, Timothy Lillicrap, Jimmy Ba, Mohammad Norouzi. (2) Date: arXiv lists v1 "Submitted on 3 December 2019." (3) Venue: The claim that arXiv lists no venue comment is true, but ICLR 2020 publication is independently confirmed by OpenReview (forum id=S1lOTC4tDS, ICLR 2020 Conference) and by the official ICLR 2020 virtual conference poster page (iclr.cc/virtual_2020/poster_S1lOTC4tDS.html). (4) Mechanism: The abstract states verbatim that Dreamer "solves long-horizon tasks from images purely by latent imagination" and works by "propagating analytic gradients of learned state values back through trajectories imagined in the compact state space of a learned world model." The body confirms it learns both an action model (policy) and a value model (expected imagined rewards), using reparameterized sampling to backpropagate analytic gradients through the learned latent dynamics. One trivial caveat: the paper itself names the agent "Dreamer," not "DreamerV1" — the version suffix is a later retronym coined after DreamerV2/V3, not a factual error in the claim. Both claimed source URLs are genuine and contain the stated content.

verifiedClaims.claim: DreamerV1's world model is a PlaNet-derived RSSM with ~30-dimensional diagonal-Gaussian latent states learned via image reconstruction; the actor (tanh-Gaussian policy) and critic (value) are trained over imagination horizon H=15 using lambda-returns (gamma=0.99, lambda=0.95), and the actor maximizes value by backpropagating analytic gradients through the learned dynamics rather than using Reinforce or derivative-free planning.
verifiedClaims.evidence: Every component is confirmed by verbatim text in the cited primary source (arXiv:1912.01603, "Dream to Control," the DreamerV1 paper) and independently corroborated by the author's official reference code (github.com/danijar/dreamer). VERBATIM QUOTES FROM THE PAPER: (a) RSSM from PlaNet: "We implement the transition model as a recurrent state space model (RSSM; Hafner et al., 2018)" (PlaNet). (b) Latent: "Distributions in latent space are 30-dimensional diagonal Gaussians." (c) World model learned by reconstructing images (observation model q(o|s)). (d) Policy: "The action model outputs a tanh-transformed Gaussian (Haarnoja et al., 2018) with sufficient statistics predicted by the neural network." (e) Horizon: "The imagination horizon is H=15 and the same trajectories are used to update both action and value models." (f) Returns: "We compute the V_lambda targets with gamma=0.99 and lambda=0.95." (g) Optimization: "The action model uses analytic gradients through the learned dynamics to maximize the value estimates," explicitly contrasted with Reinforce: "Agents using Reinforce gradients (Williams, 1992), such as A3C and PPO ... while Dreamer backpropagates through the value model." CODE CORROBORATION (danijar/dreamer dreamer.py): config.discount = 0.99; config.disclam (lambda) = 0.95; config.horizon = 15; config.action_dist = 'tanh_normal'; lambda-returns computed with lambda_=disclam. WebSearch (TorchRL docs) further corroborates horizon default 15, actor loss = negative average lambda-return, and analytic-gradient propagation. MINOR NUANCE (does not refute): the 30-dim diagonal Gaussian is specifically the STOCHASTIC part of the RSSM state, which also includes a deterministic GRU recurrent component; the claim's "~30-dimensional diagonal-Gaussian latent states" correctly refers to that stochastic latent. Attempts to refute (checking for REINFORCE/CEM usage in the actor) instead confirmed the paper explicitly rejects those in favor of analytic gradients. No contradicting evidence found.

title: Generative interactive environments / neural game engines
summary: Generative interactive environments ("neural game engines") are world models that synthesize playable video frame-by-frame, conditioned on user actions, with no underlying game engine. DeepMind's Genie line defines the frontier. Genie 1 (arXiv 2402.15391, Feb 2024) is an 11B-param foundation world model with three parts—a spatiotemporal (ST-transformer) video tokenizer, a latent action model (learning latent actions unsupervised), and an autoregressive dynamics model—trained on 200,000+ hours of unlabelled internet 2D-platformer video; it ran at ~1 FPS, too slow to play. Genie 2 (Dec 4, 2024) is an autoregressive latent-diffusion + causal transformer dynamics model prompted from a single image (often Imagen 3), 360p, keyboard/mouse control, classifier-free guidance, consistent for "up to a minute" but typically 10–20s; pairs with the SIMA agent. Genie 3 (Aug 5, 2025) is the first real-time playable Genie: 720p, 24 FPS (~41ms/frame), several minutes of interaction, ~1-minute visual memory, text-to-world plus "promptable world events"; shipped as "Project Genie" to US AI Ultra subscribers on Jan 29, 2026 (capped at 60s, promptable events excluded). Google GameNGen (arXiv 2408.14837, Aug 2024, ICLR 2025) repurposes Stable Diffusion v1.4 to simulate DOOM at 20 FPS on a single TPU; PSNR 29.4; humans barely beat chance distinguishing it after 5 min; trained by recording a PPO RL agent then training a diffusion model conditioned on past frames/actions, with Gaussian noise augmentation on context frames to fight autoregressive drift, plus decoder fine-tuning. Decart/Etched Oasis (Oct 31, 2024) is an open-source (500M) DiT + ViT autoencoder Minecraft world model, 20 FPS (frame every 0.04s), using Diffusion Forcing and dynamic noising; optimized for Etched's Sohu ASIC. DIAMOND (NeurIPS 2024 spotlight, arXiv 2405.12399) is a diffusion world model (EDM/Karras, 3 denoising steps) for RL achieving 1.46 mean HNS on Atari 100k (beating IRIS 1.046, DreamerV3 1.097, superhuman on 11 games); scaled from 4.4M params (Atari) to 381M for a CS:GO neural engine (87h data, 10Hz on RTX 3090). Microsoft Muse/WHAM (Nature, Feb 2025, 1.6B) models Bleeding Edge from 7 years of gameplay; the WHAMM (MaskGIT) variant (Apr 2025) hits 10+ FPS at 640×360. The central tension throughout is the latency↔consistency tradeoff: autoregressive rollouts compound errors (drift), mitigated by noise-augmented context (GameNGen), Diffusion Forcing/dynamic noising (Oasis), and explicit memory (Genie 3).

keyClaims.claim: Genie 1 (arXiv 2402.15391, submitted Feb 23 2024, lead author Jake Bruce) is an 11B-parameter foundation world model composed of three components: a spatiotemporal (ST-transformer) video tokenizer, a latent action model, and an autoregressive dynamics model, trained unsupervised on 200,000+ hours of unlabelled publicly-available internet gaming video with no ground-truth action labels.

Genie 1's learned latent action space lets users act in generated worlds frame-by-frame, and it can be prompted from text, synthetic images, photographs, and sketches; however it generated only ~1 frame per second, which Wikipedia notes made the worlds effectively unplayable as games. Genie 1 was announced March 2024.

Genie 2 (released December 4, 2024) is an autoregressive latent diffusion model trained on a large video dataset, using an autoencoder plus a large transformer dynamics model with a causal mask (like an LLM); it is prompted from a single image (real or generated by Imagen 3) and controlled with keyboard and mouse inputs, using classifier-free guidance to improve action controllability.

Genie 2 can generate consistent worlds for up to a minute, with the majority of shown examples lasting 10-20 seconds, at 360p resolution; it shows emergent physics (water, gravity, smoke), lighting/reflections, NPC behavior, and memory of out-of-view parts of the world, and works with the SIMA agent.

Genie 3 (announced August 5, 2025) is the first real-time-interactive Genie: it renders navigable worlds at 720p and 24 frames per second (updating each frame in ~41ms), supports a few minutes of continuous interaction, and has visual memory extending as far back as about one minute, a step up from Genie 2's ~10-20s consistency.

Genie 3 introduces 'promptable world events' (changing weather, adding objects/characters via text mid-interaction) to expand counterfactual scenarios for agent training, and was demonstrated with the SIMA agent navigating and completing tasks without explicit knowledge of the underlying world model. It launched as a limited research preview.

Genie 3's stated limitations include a limited agent action space, difficulty with multi-agent interactions, inability to simulate real-world locations with perfect geographic accuracy, poor in-world text rendering, and lack of support for extended (multi-hour) interaction.

Genie 3 was released to the public as 'Project Genie' on January 29, 2026, available only to Google AI Ultra subscribers in the US (18+), powered by Genie 3, Nano Banana Pro and Gemini; it offers world sketching, exploration, and remixing but caps exploration at 60 seconds and excludes the promptable world-events feature shown in August 2025.

Google GameNGen ('Diffusion Models Are Real-Time Game Engines', arXiv 2408.14837, submitted Aug 27 2024, accepted ICLR 2025; authors Valevski, Leviathan, Arar, Fruchter) simulates DOOM by repurposing Stable Diffusion v1.4 (whose autoencoder compresses 8x8 pixel patches into 4 latent channels), running at over 20 frames per second on a single TPU.

GameNGen achieves next-frame-prediction PSNR of 29.4 (comparable to lossy JPEG), and human raters are only slightly better than random chance at distinguishing real gameplay clips from the simulation even after 5 minutes of autoregressive generation.

GameNGen is trained in two phases: (1) an RL agent learns to play DOOM and its sessions are recorded, (2) a diffusion model is trained to predict the next frame conditioned on past frames and actions. Stability over long autoregressive trajectories is achieved by adding Gaussian noise to encoded context frames (conditioning augmentation), and the latent autoencoder's decoder is fine-tuned with MSE loss to improve detail/text fidelity.

Decart and Etched's Oasis (released October 31, 2024) is the first playable, real-time, open-world AI model; it is a latent diffusion world model of Minecraft using a Transformer-based architecture (ViT spatial autoencoder + DiT diffusion backbone), generating frames autoregressively from keyboard/mouse input with no original Minecraft code or textures.

Oasis generates real-time output at 20 frames per second (a new frame every 0.04 seconds), over 100x faster than comparable text-to-video models; it uses the Diffusion Forcing training method plus dynamic noising to address temporal stability and error accumulation. A 500M-parameter model and weights are open-sourced on Hugging Face (Etched/oasis-500m), with a larger checkpoint used in the live demo, and it is optimized for Etched's Sohu Transformer ASIC.
Oasis's stated limitations include fuzzy video in the distance, weak temporal consistency for uncertain objects, imprecise inventory control, and difficulties over long contexts.

DIAMOND ('DIffusion As a Model Of eNvironment Dreams', arXiv 2405.12399, NeurIPS 2024 Spotlight, Alonso et al.) trains an RL agent inside a diffusion world model built on the EDM formulation (Karras et al. 2022) rather than DDPM, using only 3 denoising steps (n=3) at inference, motivated by the argument that compressing into discrete latents can discard visual details important for RL.
DIAMOND achieves a mean human-normalized score of 1.46 on the Atari 100k benchmark (superhuman on 11 games), beating IRIS (1.046) and DreamerV3 (1.097); its U-Net uses ~4M parameters for Atari.

DIAMOND's diffusion world model was also trained as a standalone interactive neural game engine for CS:GO using 87 hours of static human gameplay (no RL agent), scaling the U-Net to 381M parameters (including a 51M upsampler), performing dynamics prediction at low resolution (56x30) before upsampling, and running at 10Hz on an RTX 3090.

Microsoft's Muse (the first World and Human Action Model, WHAM-1.6B) was published in Nature (February 2025), trained on over 1 billion images and controller actions (~7 years of human gameplay) from Xbox's Bleeding Edge with Ninja Theory; it can run as a world model, a behavior policy, or generate both, and Microsoft open-sourced weights and the WHAM Demonstrator.

Microsoft's WHAMM (World and Human Action MaskGIT Model, April 4, 2025) replaces WHAM-1.6B's one-token-at-a-time autoregressive generation with a MaskGIT setup that emits all tokens for an image at once, reaching 10+ FPS at 640x360 (vs WHAM-1.6B's ~1 FPS at 300x180); it uses a ~500M backbone transformer plus a ~250M refinement transformer, a 9-frame (0.9s) context, and was trained on just 1 week of Bleeding Edge data.

The recurring core challenge in these systems is the latency-vs-consistency tradeoff: autoregressive video rollouts suffer exposure bias / distribution drift where errors compound over long horizons. Mitigations include GameNGen's noise-augmented context frames, Oasis's Diffusion Forcing / dynamic noising, and newer methods such as BAgger (Backwards Aggregation, arXiv 2512.12080, Dec 2025) that teach models to recover from their own rollout mistakes.
In February 2026, Waymo adopted Genie 3 to build a specialized Waymo World Model for autonomous-driving simulation, illustrating world models' use beyond gaming as agent/robot training simulators.

openQuestions: Genie 1/2/3 parameter counts and architectures beyond Genie 1's 11B are undisclosed by DeepMind; resolution/FPS for Genie 1 (reported ~1 FPS, 16x16-class) and exact Genie 3 model size remain unconfirmed by primary sources.
Whether Genie 3's ~1-minute visual memory is a hard architectural limit or a deliberate cap, and how it is implemented (explicit memory vs context window) is not publicly detailed.

Exact context-window sizes for GameNGen (number of past frames/actions conditioned on) and Oasis were not confirmed from primary abstracts read here; commonly cited as ~64 frames for GameNGen but needs paper-body verification.

No standardized, widely-adopted benchmark yet quantifies the latency-consistency-fidelity tradeoff across these systems; WorldModelBench (CVPR 2025) is nascent and cross-system comparisons remain largely qualitative.

Commercial/training-data provenance and licensing for game-imitating models (DOOM, Minecraft, Bleeding Edge, CS:GO) raise unresolved IP questions, especially for Oasis (no Minecraft code but trained to reproduce it) and GameNGen.

How well real-time world models actually transfer as agent/robot training simulators (Genie 3 + SIMA, Waymo World Model) at scale is asserted but not yet demonstrated with strong quantitative downstream results in primary sources.

UNSUPERVISED / NO ACTION LABELS: Confirmed verbatim — "trained in an unsupervised manner from unlabelled Internet videos" and "despite training without any ground-truth action labels."

200,000+ HOURS OF INTERNET GAMING VIDEO: The paper's introduction states verbatim "Genie is trained from a large dataset of over 200,000 hours of publicly available Internet gaming videos," so the claim's wording faithfully matches the paper's own headline framing.

ONE NUANCE (does not refute the claim, which mirrors the paper's abstract language): While the 200,000+ hours figure is the paper's own stated headline number for the data, the final 11B model was actually trained on a QUALITY-FILTERED subset — the paper says the 11B model used "a filtered set of 30,000 hours of Internet gameplay videos from hundreds of 2D platformer games" ("The final dataset contains 6.8M 16s video clips (30k hours)"). The 200K+ figure was the larger collected/keyword-filtered pool before a quality classifier reduced it to ~12% (~30k hours). So "trained on 200,000+ hours" is technically a slight over-statement of what the released 11B model directly trained on, but it precisely reproduces the language used in the paper's own abstract/intro, so the claim is supported as written.

verifiedClaims.claim: Genie 1's learned latent action space lets users act in generated worlds frame-by-frame; it can be prompted from text, synthetic images, photographs, and sketches; it generated only ~1 frame per second, which Wikipedia notes made the worlds effectively unplayable as games; announced March 2024.
verifiedClaims.evidence:
Nearly all of the claim is directly confirmed by both cited primary sources, but the announcement date is imprecise.

1) Latent action space + frame-by-frame control — CONFIRMED by arXiv:2402.15391 ("Genie: Generative Interactive Environments," 11B-param model). The abstract states "the resulting learned latent action space facilitates training agents to imitate behaviors from unseen videos" and that the model lets users "act in the generated environments on a frame-by-frame basis despite training without any ground-truth action labels."

2) Prompt modalities — CONFIRMED verbatim by the same abstract: Genie "can be prompted to generate an endless variety of action-controllable virtual worlds described through text, synthetic images, photographs, and even sketches." This matches the claim's four modalities exactly.

3) ~1 FPS / unplayable — CONFIRMED verbatim by the Wikipedia article (Genie (world model)): "The original Genie generated worlds at only one frame per second, which made worlds unplayable as video games." This precisely supports both the frame-rate figure and the attribution to Wikipedia regarding unplayability.

4) "Announced March 2024" — ONLY PARTIALLY supported and likely inaccurate. Wikipedia's wording does say "The original Genie model was introduced in March 2024," so the claim faithfully echoes that page. However, the more authoritative primary source contradicts it: the arXiv paper's [v1] submission is dated "Fri, 23 Feb 2024," and DeepMind's own announcement and reporting place the unveiling in late February 2024 (Feb 23, 2024). So the actual announcement was February 2024, not March; "March 2024" is off by roughly a week-to-a-month and appears to be a Wikipedia imprecision the claim inherited.

Net: every substantive technical and quantitative claim is solidly supported by the cited primary sources; only the announcement month is wrong relative to the primary record, which is why this is partially- rather than fully-supported.

title: Video generation as world simulation & the physics debate
summary: The "video generation as world simulation" debate crystallized around OpenAI's February 2024 Sora report, titled "Video generation models as world simulators," which hypothesized that scaling video models is "a promising path towards building general purpose simulators of the physical world." Sora is a diffusion transformer (DiT) operating on spacetime patches of compressed video latents, generating up to 60s clips. OpenAI claimed emergent properties (3D consistency, long-range coherence/object permanence, world-interaction, Minecraft simulation) while admitting it fails to model basic physics like glass shattering. This framing recurs across labs: Google Veo 3 (May 2025, native audio, 4K), Runway Gen-3 Alpha (2024) and Gen-4 (Mar 2025) explicitly pursuing "General World Models," Luma (Dream Machine/Ray2) training "multimodal world models," and Genie 2/3 (Dec 2024/Aug 2025), DeepMind's interactive auto-regressive world models (Genie 3: 720p, 24fps, real-time, ~1 min consistency). NVIDIA Cosmos (Jan 2025) is a "World Foundation Model" platform for Physical AI (robotics/AV), with diffusion (7B/14B) and autoregressive (4B-13B) families trained on ~20M hours / 9000T tokens, plus tokenizers and Cosmos Reason/Predict/Transfer. AGAINST the "world model" claim: the central academic critique is ByteDance Seed's "How Far is Video Generation from World Model: A Physical Law Perspective" (Nov 2024, ICML 2025), showing DiT models achieve near-perfect in-distribution but fail out-of-distribution generalization, exhibiting "case-based" (nearest-training-example) rather than rule-based learning, with attribute priority color>>size>>velocity>>shape — concluding scaling alone is insufficient. Google DeepMind's Physics-IQ (Jan 2025) found no correlation between visual realism and physical understanding (r=-0.46); Sora scored highest on realism but lowest on physics (8.7%). VideoPhy/VideoPhy-2 benchmarks show best models hit only ~40-55% joint physical-commonsense. Gary Marcus and others argue Sora learns statistical regularities, not causal physics. FOR: DeepMind's "Video models are zero-shot learners and reasoners" (Sep 2025) argues Veo 3 is becoming a generalist vision foundation model via "chain-of-frames," solving mazes (78% pass@10 vs Veo 2's 14%). Sora 2 (Sep 2025) markedly improved physics (balls rebound vs teleport).

keyClaims.claim: OpenAI's Feb 2024 Sora report 'Video generation models as world simulators' framed video generation as a path to physical-world simulation: 'scaling video generation models is a promising path towards building general purpose simulators of the physical world' and 'continued scaling of video models is a promising path towards the development of highly-capable simulators of the physical and digital world.' Sora is a diffusion transformer operating on spacetime latent patches, generating up to 60s of high-fidelity video.

OpenAI claimed Sora exhibits emergent simulation capabilities purely from scale: 3D consistency, long-range coherence and object permanence, interacting-with-the-world effects (e.g. a painter leaving strokes that persist on canvas, eating a burger leaving bite marks), and simulating digital worlds — 'Sora can simultaneously control the player in Minecraft with a basic policy while also rendering the world and its dynamics in high fidelity.'

OpenAI explicitly admitted Sora's physics limitations in the same report: it 'does not accurately model the physics of many basic interactions, like glass shattering,' and other interactions like eating food do not always yield correct changes in object state; it exhibits incoherent dynamics over long durations and spontaneous object appearances.

ByteDance Seed's 'How Far is Video Generation from World Model: A Physical Law Perspective' (arXiv 2411.02385, Nov 2024; ICML 2025) is the central academic critique: using a deterministic 2D Box2D simulator (uniform motion/inertia, elastic collision, parabolic motion), scaling DiT models from 22.5M to 456M params and data from 30K to 3M videos, they found near-perfect in-distribution generalization but failure out-of-distribution (uniform motion velocity error rose from ID 0.012 to OOD 0.427, ~35x). They concluded 'scaling alone is insufficient for video generation models to uncover fundamental physical laws.'

The ByteDance study's mechanistic finding is that video models generalize by 'case-based' retrieval (mimicking the nearest training example) rather than abstracting rules: a model trained only on rightward motion produced physically impossible reversed velocities for slow OOD balls by copying horizontally-flipped training cases. The model's reference-matching priority order is color >> size >> velocity >> shape, explaining why shape is poorly preserved (small pixel change). Combinatorial generalization did improve with scale (abnormal rate dropped from 67% with 6 templates to 10% with 60 templates).

Google DeepMind's Physics-IQ benchmark (Motamed et al., arXiv 2501.09038, Jan 2025; 396 4K videos, 66 scenarios, models given 3s and must predict 5s) found visual realism and physical understanding are not correlated (Pearson r=-0.46, p=.247). Physics-IQ scores: VideoPoet (multiframe) 24.1% (best), Runway Gen-3 18.4%, Lumiere 18.2%, Stable Video Diffusion 13.5%, Pika 1.0 9.5%, Sora 8.7% (worst on physics despite top MLLM visual-realism score 55.6%). Conclusion: 'visual realism does not imply physical understanding.'

VideoPhy (arXiv 2406.03520, ICLR 2025, 688 captions across solid/fluid material interactions) found the best model CogVideoX-5B satisfied both caption adherence and physical commonsense for only 39.6% of instances. VideoPhy-2 (arXiv 2503.06800, 200 actions) found best model Wan2.2-27B-A14B reached only 55.4% joint score (Wan2.1-14B 32.6%), dropping to 22% on the hard subset; models struggle most with conservation laws (mass, momentum).

On the FOR side, Google DeepMind's 'Video models are zero-shot learners and reasoners' (Wiedemer et al., arXiv 2509.20328, Sep 2025) argues Veo 3 is becoming a generalist vision foundation model like LLMs did for NLP, via 'chain-of-frames' (CoF) reasoning. Tested on 62 qualitative tasks / 7 quantitative categories (18,384 videos), Veo 3 shows large gains over Veo 2 within ~6 months: maze solving (5x5) 78% pass@10 vs Veo 2's 14%; object extraction 93% vs near-chance; edge detection 0.77 pass@10; segmentation 0.74 mIoU.

Google Veo 3 launched May 20, 2025 at Google I/O as the first major video model with natively-generated synchronized audio (dialogue, SFX, ambient), up to 4K, 24fps, 48kHz stereo, 4-8s clips, marketed for realistic physics (water, fabric, dynamics). Veo 3.1 is the current iteration.

Runway frames its video models as steps toward 'General World Models' (GWMs) that build internal representations of environments. Gen-3 Alpha (2024) improved fidelity, consistency, and physically-plausible motion. Gen-4 (announced Mar 31, 2025) headlined 'world consistency' via a References system for consistent characters/objects/scenes across shots without fine-tuning, enabling coherent regeneration of a setting from different angles.

Luma AI (Dream Machine, Ray2) is pivoting from video generation to training 'multimodal world models' that jointly learn from video, audio, and language; Ray2 used ~10x the compute of Ray and a new multimodal architecture. Luma's research includes 'Inductive Moment Matching' (few-step generation, optimizing in distribution space) by Jiaming Song, and the company raised Saudi (HUMAIN) backing for multimodal foundation models / 'worldsim'.

NVIDIA Cosmos (arXiv 2501.03575, announced CES Jan 6-7 2025) is a 'World Foundation Model' (WFM) platform for Physical AI (robotics, autonomous driving), defining a WFM as predicting future observation x_{t+1} from past observations and a current perturbation (action/text/random). It ships two pre-trained families: diffusion (Cosmos-1.0-Diffusion-7B/14B Text2World, fine-tuned to Video2World) and autoregressive (4B/5B/12B/13B), plus a Cosmos Tokenizer suite (8x8/16x16 spatial, 4x/8x/16x temporal compression).

Cosmos was trained on ~20M hours of raw video (~100M curated 2-60s clips; ~9000 trillion / 9000T tokens) using 10,000 NVIDIA H100 GPUs over three months, with data spanning driving (11%), hand motion (16%), human motion (10%), spatial navigation (16%), nature (20%), etc. Released under NVIDIA Open Model License. At GTC (Mar 18, 2025) NVIDIA expanded the platform with Cosmos Reason (reasoning VLM for data curation), Cosmos Predict 2/2.5, and Cosmos Transfer; adopters include 1X, Agility Robotics, Figure AI, Skild AI, Uber.

DeepMind Genie 2 (Dec 4, 2024) is a 'large-scale foundation world model' generating action-controllable, playable 3D environments from a single image, consistent for 'up to a minute' (Ars Technica observed 10-20s in practice). Genie 3 (Aug 5, 2025) is the first real-time interactive world model: 720p, 24fps, navigable in real time, consistent for 'several minutes' with visual memory '~one minute ago,' supports 'promptable world events' (change weather, add objects). Its consistency is an 'emergent capability' not built on explicit 3D (NeRF/Gaussian Splatting) representations; tested with the SIMA agent and framed as 'critical' for the 'push toward AGI.' Released publicly as Project Genie on Jan 29, 2026.

Critics (notably Gary Marcus) argue Sora is 'at best a semi-reliable guide to how the world looks,' not how it works: it fails object permanence (objects/limbs winking in and out as pixel predictions, not entity states), merges similar interacting objects, and learned statistical regularities consistent with physics rather than causal models / equations. The argument: pixel-correlation across frames is mistaken for object permanence.

Yann LeCun's counter-position is architectural: predicting the future pixel-by-pixel yields only a 'blurry average' and cannot reach the abstraction needed for action; he argues this is a structural limitation, not a scale problem. His Joint Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA / V-JEPA 2) predicts in abstract latent representation space, deliberately discarding unpredictable visual detail — V-JEPA 2 plans actions in seconds vs minutes for pixel-space approaches.

Sora 2 (released Sep 30, 2025) markedly improved physics, addressing earlier critiques: where prior models would teleport a basketball into the hoop on a miss, Sora 2 makes the ball rebound off the backboard; dropped objects accelerate near real gravity, bounces lose energy, throws follow parabolic trajectories. OpenAI states 'mistakes' now resemble errors of an implicit internal agent, and reiterates that 'more advanced world simulation capabilities' are 'critical for training AI models that deeply understand the physical world.'

openQuestions: Is the OOD/'case-based generalization' failure shown by ByteDance a fundamental limit of pixel/latent diffusion, or an artifact of toy 2D Box2D settings that frontier models like Sora 2 / Veo 3 partly overcome with web-scale data?

Does Sora 2's visibly improved physics (gravity, rebounds, energy loss) reflect genuine internalized dynamics / an 'implicit agent,' or just a denser interpolation over more training data that would still fail systematic OOD tests?

Are interactive, action-conditioned world models (Genie 3, Cosmos Video2World) categorically closer to 'true' world models than passive text-to-video, since they must respond coherently to user/agent actions and maintain state?

Will the LeCun/JEPA thesis hold — that latent-space prediction is necessary and pixel-space video generation is structurally incapable of robust planning — or will scaled generative video plus 'chain-of-frames' reasoning (Veo 3) suffice for vision foundation models?
Do downstream Physical AI results (Cosmos-trained robots/AVs, synthetic data) actually transfer to the real world, validating WFMs as practical simulators despite benchmark physics failures?

Why does visual realism anti-correlate with physics scores (Physics-IQ r=-0.46) — does optimizing perceptual quality actively trade off against dynamical fidelity, and can joint objectives or physics-alignment methods (VideoREPA, inference-time alignment) close the gap?

As benchmarks proliferate (Physics-IQ, VideoPhy-2, PhyGenBench, Morpheus, PhyWorldBench), is there a converging, contamination-resistant standard for 'physical understanding,' or are improving scores partly benchmark overfitting?

title: JEPA & self-supervised predictive world models
summary: JEPA (Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture) is Yann LeCun's proposed path to "autonomous machine intelligence," laid out in his 2022 position paper "A Path Towards Autonomous Machine Intelligence" (OpenReview, June 2022). The core thesis: instead of generative models that predict raw inputs (pixels, tokens), build world models that predict in an abstract REPRESENTATION space. LeCun frames this as an energy-based model (EBM): the system assigns low energy when a predicted representation s_y matches an encoded target, plus a latent variable z to capture genuinely unpredictable/multimodal information. He prefers EBMs over probabilistic generative models because normalizing high-dimensional distributions is intractable, and because generative pixel-predictors "waste capacity" modeling unpredictable detail (flickering leaves, textures) and produce blurry, averaged outputs; a JEPA can simply ignore unpredictable detail and keep only what is predictable. The full vision is a 6-module cognitive architecture (configurator, perception, world model, short-term memory, actor, cost), with Mode-1 (reactive) and Mode-2 (deliberate planning via gradient-based or sampling optimization through the world model), and Hierarchical JEPA (H-JEPA) for multi-timescale abstraction. Meta operationalized this in a model lineage: I-JEPA (images, CVPR 2023; ViT-Huge/14 on ImageNet in <72h on 16 A100s; SOTA linear-probe with ~12 labels/class), V-JEPA (video, Apr 2024; ViT-H/16, 2M videos, frozen-eval 81.9% K400 / 72.2% SSv2 / 77.9% ImageNet, no pixel reconstruction), and V-JEPA 2 (June 11 2025; 1.2B-param ViT-g, VideoMix22M = >1M hours video + 1M images). V-JEPA 2 adds V-JEPA 2-AC, a ~300M action-conditioned world model post-trained on just 62 hours of unlabeled DROID robot video, enabling zero-shot pick-and-place on unseen Franka arms via model-predictive control with the Cross-Entropy Method (~16s/action vs ~4min for Nvidia Cosmos; 65-80% success). Meta released 3 physical-reasoning benchmarks (IntPhys 2, MVPBench/Minimal Video Pairs, CausalVQA) where humans score 85-95% but models near chance. Collapse (the central JEPA failure mode) is prevented via EMA teacher + regularizers like VICReg. In Nov 2025 LeCun left Meta; his Paris startup AMI Labs raised a $1.03B seed (March 2026) to build JEPA-based world models.

keyClaims.claim: LeCun's foundational vision document is the 2022 position paper 'A Path Towards Autonomous Machine Intelligence,' which introduces JEPA and a 6-module cognitive architecture (configurator, perception, world model, short-term memory, actor, cost). The actor finds an optimal action sequence minimizing estimated future cost, operating in reactive Mode-1 and deliberative planning Mode-2.

JEPA is an energy-based model operating in representation space: encoders map inputs x and y to abstract representations s_x and s_y, a predictor estimates s_y from s_x, and a latent variable z captures unpredictable information. It assigns low energy (low error) when predicted and target representations match, and crucially avoids reconstructing the full input space.

LeCun argues against generative pixel prediction because the world is unpredictable: a generative model trying to predict every pixel of future frames wastes capacity modeling chaotic high-entropy detail (flickering leaves, textures) and produces blurry averaged predictions, whereas a JEPA predicts the abstract state and can 'choose to ignore' details that are not easily predictable, keeping only low-entropy structural information.

LeCun prefers energy-based models over probabilistic generative models because normalizing high-dimensional probability distributions is computationally intractable; EBMs operate on unnormalized energy scores and can represent multimodal distributions (multiple plausible futures) without normalization overhead.

LeCun publicly argues that pure autoregressive LLMs are a 'dead end' toward human-level AI: he models them as exponentially diverging, where the probability a length-n answer is fully correct is roughly (1-e)^n, so errors compound and the model cannot be fully corrected; this is his explanation for hallucination. He stated 'Pure Auto-Regressive LLMs are a dead end' (Sept 2024) and reiterated it at the Feb 2025 AI Action Summit and a talk titled 'Mathematical Obstacles on the Way to Human-Level AI.'

I-JEPA (Image JEPA, CVPR 2023, arXiv:2301.08243) predicts representations of target blocks from a single context block within the same image using a ViT encoder + predictor. It avoids hand-crafted data augmentation and is computationally efficient: a ViT-Huge/14 was trained on ImageNet with 16 A100 GPUs in under 72 hours. Authors: Assran, Duval, Misra, Bojanowski, Vincent, Rabbat, LeCun, Ballas.

I-JEPA's design avoids the failure of generative methods like MAE that try to predict 'every bit of missing information' and thus 'focus too much on irrelevant details' (e.g. struggling to generate hands). The masking strategy is critical: target blocks must be large/semantic and the context block spatially distributed and informative. I-JEPA reached strong ImageNet linear-probe performance using only ~12 labeled examples per class and excelled at depth prediction and object counting.

The original V-JEPA (arXiv:2404.08471, submitted Feb 15 2024) demonstrated feature prediction as a standalone self-supervised objective for video, with NO pretrained image encoders, text, negative examples, or reconstruction. Trained on 2 million public videos. A frozen ViT-H/16 backbone achieved 81.9% on Kinetics-400, 72.2% on Something-Something-v2, and 77.9% on ImageNet-1K. Authors include Bardes, Garrido, Ponce, Chen, Rabbat, LeCun, Assran, Ballas.

V-JEPA 2 (arXiv:2506.09985, released June 11 2025) is a ~1.2B-parameter model (ViT-g, ~1B+ encoder) pretrained on VideoMix22M (22M samples, >1 million hours of internet video plus 1M ImageNet images). Sources include Something-Something v2, Kinetics 400/600/700, HowTo100M, and a cluster-curated subset of YT-Temporal-1B. Lead author Mido Assran; ~30 authors including Yann LeCun.

V-JEPA 2 video architecture details: inputs patchified into tubelets of size 2x16x16 (TxHxW), default 16-frame clips at 256x256, progressively scaled to 64 frames at 384x384 during a cooldown phase, using a 3D extension of 1D-RoPE position embeddings. Model sizes: ViT-L 300M, ViT-H 600M, ViT-g 1B parameters.

V-JEPA 2 understanding/anticipation benchmark results (ViT-g at 384 resolution): 77.3% top-1 on Something-Something v2 (motion), 39.7 recall-at-5 on Epic-Kitchens-100 action anticipation (surpassing prior task-specific models), 90.2% on Diving-48. At 8B scale aligned with an LLM: 84.0% on PerceptionTest and 76.9% on TempCompass video QA.

V-JEPA 2-AC is an action-conditioned world model: a ~300M-parameter block-causal transformer (24 layers, 16 heads, 1024 hidden dim) post-trained on a FROZEN V-JEPA 2 encoder using only 62 hours of unlabeled robot video (~23k Franka Panda trajectories) from the DROID dataset. Actions are a 7-D vector (3D end-effector position, 3D orientation, gripper state); trained with teacher-forcing plus 2-step rollout losses.

V-JEPA 2-AC enables zero-shot robot planning via model-predictive control using the Cross-Entropy Method (energy minimization in latent space) with receding-horizon control (1-4 steps), deployed on Franka arms in new labs using a single uncalibrated monocular RGB camera and WITHOUT any data collection from those robots. Per-action planning time is ~16 seconds versus ~4 minutes for Nvidia Cosmos.

V-JEPA 2-AC robotics success rates: reach tasks succeed within <4 cm of goal (reported ~100% on reach); pick-and-place of new objects in new/unseen environments succeeds 65-80%. In a head-to-head, V-JEPA 2-AC achieved 80% (cup) and 50% (box) pick-and-place in Lab 2 versus 0% for Cosmos on both.

Alongside V-JEPA 2, Meta released three physical-reasoning benchmarks: IntPhys 2 (physically plausible vs implausible scenarios), MVPBench / Minimal Video Pairs (minimal-change paired multiple-choice on physical understanding), and CausalVQA (cause-effect, counterfactual, anticipation). Humans score 85-95% accuracy while current video models perform at or near chance (notably on IntPhys 2), exposing a large human-model gap in physical reasoning.

The central failure mode of JEPA-style joint-embedding methods is representation collapse (encoder outputs trivial constant representations). It is prevented via an EMA (exponential moving average) teacher encoder plus regularizers; VICReg (Variance-Invariance-Covariance Regularization) maintains per-dimension variance across a batch and decorrelates features to maximize embedding information content and avoid collapse.
V-JEPA 2 was open-sourced on GitHub and Hugging Face under a permissive license for commercial and research use, released June 11 2025.

A follow-up, V-JEPA 2.1 (arXiv:2603.14482, March 15 2026, FAIR/Meta + Univ. Zaragoza), adds a dense prediction loss (supervising both masked and visible tokens), deep self-supervision across intermediate layers, a multimodal tokenizer (3D conv for video, 2D for images), the VisionMix-163M dataset (~142M images + 19M videos), and scales to a ViT-G 2B encoder, sharply improving dense-feature tasks (e.g. NYUv2 depth RMSE 0.642->0.307, ADE20K mIoU 24.4->47.9).

Yann LeCun left Meta in November 2025 after more than a decade leading FAIR, citing disagreement with Meta's LLM-centric strategy. His Paris-based startup AMI Labs (Advanced Machine Intelligence) raised a $1.03 billion seed round at a $3.5B pre-money valuation in March 2026 (the largest seed round for a European startup) to build JEPA-based world models for industrial, robotics, and healthcare applications; investors include Cathay Innovation, Greycroft, Bezos Expeditions, Nvidia, Samsung, and Toyota Ventures.

V-JEPA 2 pretraining data is heavily weighted toward web video: HowTo100M (~134K hours) and curated YT-Temporal-1B (~1.6M hours) dominate, with cluster-based retrieval curation of YT-Temporal adding +1.4 points over an uncurated baseline. Scaling ablations attribute roughly +1.0 (data 2M->22M videos), +1.5 (model 300M->1B), +0.8 (training 90K->252K iters), and +0.7 (resolution/temporal) accuracy points.

openQuestions: Whether JEPA world models scale to long-horizon, multi-step planning and complex manipulation beyond the short (1-4 step) horizons and pick-and-place tasks demonstrated by V-JEPA 2-AC, given large human-model gaps remaining on IntPhys 2 / CausalVQA.

Whether the JEPA/energy-based approach can deliver language and reasoning competence competitive with LLMs, or whether it remains complementary (perception/physical-world) rather than a wholesale replacement as LeCun argues.

How decisively LeCun's 'autoregressive LLMs are exponentially diverging / a dead end' claim holds up empirically, given pushback (e.g. arXiv:2505.24187) showing LLMs generate coherent multi-thousand-token outputs and that chain-of-thought/RL mitigate error compounding.

Whether representation-space prediction with collapse-prevention (EMA teacher, VICReg) is robust and theoretically well-grounded, versus an engineering patch around the absence of a reconstruction signal.
Whether ~16s/action planning latency and CEM-based MPC are fast and reliable enough for real-time robotic deployment versus learned/amortized policies.

How AMI Labs' planned products will differ technically from Meta's open-source V-JEPA 2 line, and whether the JEPA bet attracts a broader research ecosystem or remains concentrated in LeCun-affiliated groups.
Whether action-conditioned world models trained on tiny interaction datasets (62 hours) generalize across embodiments and tasks, or overfit to Franka-arm DROID dynamics.

LeCun's foundational vision document is the 2022 position paper 'A Path Towards Autonomous Machine Intelligence,' which introduces JEPA and a 6-module cognitive architecture (configurator, perception, world model, short-term memory, actor, cost). The actor finds an optimal action sequence minimizing estimated future cost, operating in reactive Mode-1 and deliberative planning Mode-2.</claim>
