verifiedClaims.evidence: Every substantive element of the claim is confirmed directly from the primary source — LeCun's actual paper (OpenReview id=BZ5a1r-kVsf, "A Path Towards Autonomous Machine Intelligence," Version 0.9.2, 2022-06-27, sole author Yann LeCun, June 27, 2022). (1) It is explicitly a "position paper expressing my vision" (Sec 1 Prologue). (2) It introduces JEPA/H-JEPA (stated contribution #2). (3) Figure 2 and Sec 3 give exactly the six named modules: configurator, perception, world model, cost (Intrinsic Cost + Trainable Critic sub-modules), short-term memory, actor. (4) Figure 2 caption verbatim: "The actor can find an optimal action sequence that minimizes the estimated future cost, and output the first action in the optimal sequence." (5) Sec 3.1 defines two modes: "Mode-1" (3.1.1 Reactive behavior, analogy to Kahneman System 1, no planning) and "Mode-2" (3.1.2 reasoning and planning using the world model, System 2, MPC-style action-sequence optimization). The Feb 23, 2022 Meta AI blog independently confirms the six-module architecture and JEPA. HOWEVER the claim is only partially supported because one cited source is WRONG: arxiv.org/abs/2306.02572 is NOT this 2022 position paper — it is a separate, later paper, "Introduction to Latent Variable Energy-Based Models: A Path Towards Autonomous Machine Intelligence" by Anna Dawid and Yann LeCun, submitted June 5, 2023, based on 2022 Les Houches Summer School lectures. The genuine 2022 vision paper lives on OpenReview (PDF id=BZ5a1r-kVsf), not under arxiv 2306.02572. The other two cited URLs (Meta AI blog, VentureBeat) are real and topically relevant. So the scientific content is accurate, but the claim mis-attributes the foundational document to the wrong arxiv identifier, conflating LeCun's solo 2022 position paper with the 2023 Dawid-LeCun lecture-notes paper.

verifiedClaims.claim: JEPA is an energy-based model operating in representation space: encoders map x and y to s_x and s_y, a predictor estimates s_y from s_x, a latent variable z captures unpredictable information, it assigns low energy when predicted and target representations match, and it avoids reconstructing the full input space.
verifiedClaims.evidence:
Every component of the claim is confirmed by a primary source authored by Yann LeCun himself: Dawid & LeCun, "Introduction to Latent Variable Energy-Based Models: A Path Towards Autonomous Machine Intelligence" (arXiv:2306.02572, 2023). The paper frames JEPA as combining "energy-based and latent variable models" in the "hierarchical joint embedding predictive architecture (H-JEPA)." Figure 9 caption (verbatim): "A joint embedding predictive architecture (JEPA). It consists of two parallel encoders... learning representations of x and y, i.e., sx and sy. Those encoders can learn to filter irrelevant information about x and y. The aim of JEPA is to predict sy out of sx with help of a latent variable z that can represent relevant information about y that may be missing from x. The energy is the distance between those representations." This directly confirms: (a) two encoders mapping x,y to s_x,s_y; (b) predictor estimating s_y from s_x; (c) latent variable z capturing info in y missing from x (i.e., unpredictable info — the paper says z handles "multimodality of predictions"). On low energy for matches: the paper's EBM principle is that "compatible [points] have low energy, while unlikely data points have high energy," and JEPA energy = distance between representations (low distance = match = low energy). On avoiding input-space reconstruction: "JEPAs make predictions in the representation space, allowing encoders to remove irrelevant data features," explicitly contrasted with masked autoencoders that fill in missing pixels. 

INDEPENDENT CORROBORATION: Meta's official I-JEPA blog (ai.meta.com/blog/yann-lecun-ai-model-i-jepa) states the objective is "to assign a high energy to incompatible inputs, and to assign a low energy to compatible inputs," that I-JEPA predicts "representations at a high level of abstraction rather than predicting pixel values directly," and that the predictor is "conditioned on additional (possibly latent) variables z." 

NOTE ON CLAIMED SOURCES: Of the two claimed URLs, the Meta "advances-in-ai-research" blog accurately describes the architecture (x/y -> s_x/s_y, predictor, latent z, abstract representations) but does NOT itself use the term "energy-based model." The second claimed source (thesingularityproject.ai) does explicitly make the EBM framing but is secondary commentary, not a primary source. The EBM characterization is nonetheless correct and is verified against LeCun's own primary writings. The claim is fully accurate; only the attribution of the EBM label to the first Meta blog is slightly off.

title: Spatial intelligence & 3D / persistent world models
summary: Spatial intelligence is emerging as the central organizing frame for "3D/persistent" world models, articulated most forcefully by Fei-Fei Li and operationalized by World Labs and Google DeepMind. Li's Nov 2025 essay argues LLMs are "wordsmiths in the dark; eloquent but inexperienced, knowledgeable but ungrounded," and that state-of-the-art MLLMs "rarely perform better than chance" at estimating distance, orientation, and size. She defines world models by three capabilities—generative (worlds with perceptual/geometric/physical consistency), multimodal (images, video, depth, text, gestures, actions), and interactive (output next state given an action)—and in her June 2026 "Functional Taxonomy" sorts systems into renderers (output pixels; Genie 3, RTFM), simulators (output faithful state; Marble's splats + collider meshes), and planners (output actions; VLA/world-action models). Two architectural camps dominate. (1) Explicit-3D / exportable assets: World Labs' Marble (public Nov 12, 2025) turns text/single-image/multi-image/video/panorama/coarse-3D-layout prompts into persistent, editable 3D worlds exported as 3D Gaussian splats (~2M splats .ply/.spz, plus 500k lightweight), meshes, collider meshes, and video, viewable in Unreal/Unity/Blender and on Vision Pro/Quest 3. Its persistence is structural—the geometry is fixed, not re-invented per frame. Marble builds on 3D Gaussian Splatting (Kerbl et al., SIGGRAPH 2023), which gives real-time (>=30fps) photorealistic novel-view synthesis at 1080p. (2) Learned-renderer / frame-by-frame video: DeepMind's Genie 3 (Aug 5, 2025) auto-regressively generates a navigable world at 24fps/720p for a few minutes, with ~1-minute visual memory and promptable world events; consistency is "an emergent capability" with no explicit 3D and no exportable asset. World Labs' RTFM (Oct 16, 2025) is a middle path: an autoregressive diffusion transformer that is a "learned renderer" (the KV cache implicitly represents the world), persisting large worlds via "context juggling" over pose-tagged frames on a single H100, justified via the Bitter Lesson. The why-3D-matters debate centers on persistence, exportability, geometric faithfulness for robotics/agents, and compute (Genie's frame-by-frame ~100K+ tokens/sec; an hour needs >100M tokens). World Labs raised ~$1B (~$5B valuation) in Feb 2026.

keyClaims.claim: Fei-Fei Li argues LLMs are ungrounded in the physical world, calling them 'wordsmiths in the dark; eloquent but inexperienced, knowledgeable but ungrounded,' and notes 'State-of-the-art MLLM models rarely perform better than chance on estimating distance, orientation, and size.'

Li defines spatially intelligent world models by three capabilities: Generative (generate worlds with perceptual, geometric, and physical consistency), Multimodal (process images, videos, depth maps, text instructions, gestures, or actions), and Interactive (output the next states based on input actions). She frames the goal as AI that creates with a storyteller's imagination, navigates with a first responder's fluency, and reasons about space with scientific precision.

Li's essay 'From Words to Worlds: Spatial Intelligence is AI's Next Frontier' was published November 10, 2025, and argues world models must reconcile the semantic, geometric, dynamic, and physical simultaneously, calling for a universal task function 'as simple and elegant as next-token prediction' and architectures beyond current MLLM/video-diffusion paradigms that avoid tokenizing spatial data into 1D or 2D sequences.

In her June 3, 2026 'Functional Taxonomy of World Models,' Li sorts systems into three projections of a single underlying understanding: Renderers (output pixels for human eyes; e.g., Google Genie 3 and World Labs RTFM), Simulators (output geometrically/physically/dynamically faithful state; e.g., Marble outputting Gaussian splats plus collision meshes a physics engine can operate on), and Planners (output actions; e.g., Vision-Language-Action and World Action Models).

World Labs publicly launched Marble on November 12, 2025 (after a limited beta ~September 2025), described as 'the first ever world model that can be prompted by multimodal inputs to generate and maintain consistent 3D environments.' It accepts text prompts, single images, multiple images (multi-image prompting), video, 360 panoramas, and coarse 3D layouts.

Marble exports 3D Gaussian splats (the highest-fidelity representation; full-resolution ~2 million splats in .ply or .spz, plus lightweight 500k versions for real-time playback), triangle meshes, low-fidelity collider meshes for physics, and video with pixel-accurate camera control. Exports work in Unreal, Unity, Houdini, and Blender, with native VR viewing on Apple Vision Pro and Quest 3.

Marble's editing stack includes 'Chisel' (an AI-native/hybrid 3D editor that decouples structure from style, letting users sculpt with coarse boxes/planes or imported 3D assets), object removal/touch-up/style-swap, one-step world expansion ('Click and Expand'), and a Compose tool to join multiple worlds into extremely large spaces.

Marble's persistence is structural/explicit: it produces 'stable, explorable scenes' with fixed, pre-existing 3D geometry rather than 're-inventing geometry each time you move through them,' yielding an exportable 3D asset (the Gaussian splat file). This contrasts with frame-by-frame generators whose consistency is emergent and non-exportable.

Marble limitations include degraded detail as the user moves away from the seed image, weak handling of non-photorealistic/illustration inputs (grainy, buggy results), difficulty with exterior environments, and largely static worlds lacking dynamic/moving elements and isolated objects.

Google DeepMind announced Genie 3 on August 5, 2025 as a general-purpose, real-time interactive world model running at 24 frames per second at 720p resolution, supporting a few minutes of continuous navigation with visual memory extending as far back as one minute, plus 'promptable world events' (changing weather, adding objects/characters, counterfactual scenarios).

Genie 3 generates worlds auto-regressively frame by frame (each frame accounts for the previously generated trajectory that grows with time); its consistency 'is an emergent capability' that does NOT rely on explicit 3D representations like NeRFs or Gaussian Splatting. Genie 2's memory topped out around 10 seconds, versus Genie 3's ~1 minute.

Genie 3's stated limitations include a constrained/limited action space, difficult multi-agent interactions, imperfect real-world location accuracy, poor text rendering, restricted interaction duration, plus physics inaccuracies and visual hallucinations (e.g., people walking backward). It produces a real-time video stream, not a static exportable 3D asset.

World Labs released RTFM (Real-Time Frame Model) as a research preview on October 16, 2025: an autoregressive diffusion transformer trained end-to-end on large-scale video that generates video frames in real time on a single H100 GPU, rendering persistent and 3D-consistent worlds (real and imaginary) that are 'never forgotten' when you turn your back.

RTFM is a 'learned renderer' with NO explicit 3D geometry: input frames are converted to neural-network activations (the KV cache) that implicitly represent the world, and effects like reflections, glossy surfaces, shadows, and lens flare are learned end-to-end. Each frame is tagged with a 3D pose; 'context juggling' retrieves nearby posed frames as custom context, enabling persistence of large worlds without attending to an ever-growing frame set.

World Labs frames the learned-renderer bet on compute scaling and 'The Bitter Lesson': simple methods that scale gracefully with compute dominate. They note naive 4K/60fps generation would require over 100K tokens per second, and an hour-plus of interaction would require attending to contexts of well over 100M tokens—motivating spatial-memory architecture.

3D Gaussian Splatting (Kerbl, Kopanas, Leimkuhler, Drettakis), published in ACM TOG vol 42(4), July/August 2023, represents scenes as anisotropic 3D Gaussians and uses a fast visibility-aware rasterizer to achieve real-time (>=30 fps) novel-view synthesis at 1080p for unbounded scenes with state-of-the-art visual quality and competitive training times—the representation underpinning Marble's exportable worlds.

World Labs ships Spark 2.0, its open-source 3D Gaussian Splatting renderer with a streamable Level-of-Detail system (loads low-resolution splats first, progressively filling detail like game-engine LOD), letting gigabyte-scale splat scenes open in a web page via URL with no downloads/viewer install; released April 14, 2026. World Labs also launched a World API on January 21, 2026.

World Labs raised $1 billion announced February 18, 2026, with Bloomberg reporting an ~$5 billion valuation (5x its ~$1B valuation at its September 2024 stealth exit with $230M). 2026 investors include AMD, Autodesk (a $200M strategic investment), NVIDIA, Andreessen Horowitz, Fidelity, Emerson Collective, and Sea Group. Mission: advance spatial intelligence via world models for storytelling, creativity, robotics, and scientific discovery.

On the spatial/3D-vs-2D-video debate: the explicit-3D camp (Marble) offers persistence, exportable geometric assets, and physics-ready collider meshes useful for robotics/agent simulation, while the pure-video camp (Genie 3) offers richer real-time dynamics but transient, non-exportable, sometimes physically inaccurate worlds; analysts argue embodied AI will need both—generative 3D worlds for content and efficient predictive/action-conditioned models for agent training.

Genie 3's per-month consumer access (~$249.99) is materially more expensive than Marble's freemium-to-$95/month tiers (free tier plus paid tiers up to a 'Max' tier at $95/month including commercial rights and full editing), reflecting Marble's productized authoring-tool positioning versus Genie's research-preview status.

verifiedClaims.claim: Li defines spatially intelligent world models by three capabilities (Generative, Multimodal, Interactive) and frames the goal as AI that creates with a storyteller's imagination, navigates with a first responder's fluency, and reasons about space with scientific precision.
verifiedClaims.evidence:
VERIFIED against the primary source: Fei-Fei Li, "From Words to Worlds: Spatial Intelligence is AI's Next Frontier" (drfeifei.substack.com, published Nov 10, 2025), independently corroborated by the a16z.news mirror of the same essay.

THE THREE CAPABILITIES — CONFIRMED nearly verbatim:
1. Generative: "World models can generate worlds with perceptual, geometrical, and physical consistency." (Claim says "geometric" vs. original "geometrical" — trivial.)
2. Multimodal: "World models are multimodal by design," processing inputs "whether images, videos, depth maps, text instructions, gestures, or actions." (Matches claim exactly.)
3. Interactive: "World models can output the next states based on input actions." (Matches claim exactly.)

THE FRAMING QUOTE — PARAPHRASED / PARTIALLY MISREPRESENTED. The claim presents a THREE-part framing, but the essay's actual sentence is FOUR-part: "What's the path to models capable of reasoning with the vision of Eratosthenes, engineering with the precision of an industrial designer, creating with the imagination of a storyteller, and interacting with their environment with the fluency of a first responder?"
- "creates with a storyteller's imagination" — supported ("creating with the imagination of a storyteller").
- "navigates with a first responder's fluency" — loosely supported, but the original says "interacting with their environment with the fluency of a first responder," not "navigates."
- "reasons about space with scientific precision" — NOT verbatim. It compresses two distinct original elements (Eratosthenes = reasoning/vision; industrial designer = precision) into one and drops the engineering element. "Scientific precision" and "reasons about space" do not appear as written.

Verdict: The three-capability definition is solidly supported (essentially verbatim). The framing is a paraphrase that collapses a four-part construction into three and introduces wording absent from the source, so the overall claim is partially supported rather than fully accurate. The second claimed source (x.com/drfeifei/status/1987891813387292725) could not be fetched (HTTP 402, X blocks automated access), but the Substack essay it points to is the authoritative primary source.

title: Robotics, embodied & autonomous-driving world models
summary: World models for robotics, embodied AI, and autonomous driving matured from research demos (2023) into deployed platforms (2026), driven heavily by NVIDIA and Wayve. The dominant paradigm: train a generative "world model" (video/sensor predictor) that serves as a learned simulator for generating synthetic data, evaluating policies, or planning actions. NVIDIA Cosmos (Jan 2025, arXiv 2501.03575) is the flagship platform — Cosmos-Predict (diffusion 7B/14B + autoregressive 4B-13B) trained on ~20M hours / ~100M clips with proprietary tokenizers; the Nov 2025 successor Cosmos-Predict2.5 (2B/14B, flow-based, 200M clips, RL post-training, unifies Text/Image/Video2World) and Cosmos-Transfer2.5 (ControlNet-style sim2real, 3.5x smaller than v1 yet +60% on AV 3D detection). Cosmos-Reason1 (8B/56B VLM) adds physical-commonsense/embodied reasoning. For robotics, GR00T N1 (arXiv 2503.14734, 2.2B VLA: Eagle-2 System-2 + flow-matching diffusion-transformer System-1) hit 76.8% real-robot success on Fourier GR-1; GR00T N1.5 (Jun 2025) added frozen VLM + FLARE + DreamGen, lifting real GR-1 language-following 46.6%→93.3%; N1.7 shipped by 2026 on Jetson Thor. DreamGen (arXiv 2505.12705) "neural trajectories" generalized policies to 22 novel behaviors. Driving: Wayve's GAIA lineage — GAIA-1 (9B, 2023), GAIA-2 (8.4B latent diffusion, 5-camera, ~139k hrs, Mar 2025), GAIA-3 (15B, Dec 2025, shifts to closed-loop evaluation, 5x lower synthetic-test rejection). NVIDIA Alpamayo-1 (CES Jan 2026, 10B reasoning VLA) and Waabi Copilot4D (LiDAR discrete-diffusion 4D model) push reasoning/closed-loop AV. Planning-with-learned-dynamics: DreamerV3 (Nature 2025, first to mine Minecraft diamonds from scratch), TD-MPC2 (317M, 80 tasks), V-JEPA 2-AC (Meta, 1B+ encoder, 62 hrs Droid data, zero-shot Franka pick-place 65-80%, 16s/action), DINO-WM (frozen DINOv2 features + CEM planning, 0.90 Push-T SR). Key tension: video world models give photorealism + scale but are slow (Cosmos ~4 min/action) and physically imperfect; JEPA-style latent models are fast but lower-fidelity. Sim2real is now real-deployed (Waabi trucks, Tesla robotaxi Austin Jun 2025).

keyClaims.claim: NVIDIA Cosmos World Foundation Model Platform (arXiv 2501.03575, Jan 2025) provides two model families: diffusion-based (Cosmos-1.0-Diffusion-7B and 14B Text2World/Video2World) and autoregressive (Cosmos-1.0-Autoregressive-4B/5B and 12B/13B Video2World), plus the Cosmos Tokenizer.

Cosmos was trained on a curated corpus from ~20 million hours of raw video distilled to ~100 million clips (2-60s), using ~10,000 NVIDIA H100 GPUs over three months; data mix included driving (11%), manipulation (16%), human activity (10%), spatial navigation (16%), nature (20%).

The Cosmos Tokenizer offers continuous (16-dim latent) and discrete (FSQ, ~64k vocabulary) variants at compression ratios up to 8x16x16, and is reported up to 12x faster than prior tokenizers; models released under the NVIDIA Open Model License.

Cosmos-Predict2.5 (arXiv 2511.00062, submitted Oct 28 2025) is a flow-based model at 2B and 14B scales, trained on 200M curated clips with RL-based post-training, unifying Text2World/Image2World/Video2World in one model and using Cosmos-Reason1 as a text/scene encoder; generates sequences up to 30 seconds.

Cosmos-Transfer2.5 is a ControlNet-style sim2real/real2real framework that is 3.5x smaller than Cosmos-Transfer1 (7B) yet delivers up to 60% improvement in 3D lane detection (LATR) and cuboid detection (BEVFormer) on generated multi-view AV videos versus Transfer1-7B-Sample-AV.

Cosmos-Reason1 (arXiv 2503.15558, Mar 2025) ships 8B and 56B multimodal LLMs (56B uses hybrid Mamba-MLP-Transformer); Cosmos-Reason1-56B scores 60.2% avg on the physical-commonsense benchmark (vs GPT-4o 55.6%, OpenAI o1 59.9%) and 63.7% on embodied reasoning (vs GPT-4o 53.3%); Physical AI RL adds +8.2 points to the 8B model (58.9%→67.1%).

NVIDIA GR00T N1 (arXiv 2503.14734, Mar 2025) is a 2.2B-parameter dual-system VLA: System 2 is an Eagle-2 VLM (1.34B), System 1 is a flow-matching diffusion transformer generating 16-action chunks in 63.9ms on an L40; trained on a data pyramid of 88 hrs real GR-1 teleoperation, 827 hrs neural-generated trajectories, and 6,500 hrs simulation data.

GR00T N1 achieved 76.8% average real-robot success on the Fourier GR-1 humanoid (vs 46.4% for Diffusion Policy), and 42.6% vs 10.2% in a 10%-data regime; in simulation it scored 50.0% on GR-1 Tabletop vs 32.7%/16.1% for baselines.

GR00T N1.5 (NVIDIA GEAR, Jun 11 2025) froze the VLM (upgraded to Eagle 2.5), simplified the adapter, and added the FLARE loss + DreamGen data; it raised real GR-1 language-following from 46.6% to 93.3% and overall success from 43.3% to 83.0%, and zero-shot novel-object manipulation from 0% to 15% (55% with FLARE).
NVIDIA used the GR00T-Dreams blueprint to generate synthetic training data and develop GR00T N1.5 in ~36 hours, versus nearly three months of manual human data collection.

DreamGen (arXiv 2505.12705, May 2025) is a 4-step pipeline (LoRA-fine-tune a video world model like WAN 2.1 or Cosmos, generate neural trajectories, extract pseudo-actions via IDM/LAPA, train the policy); it enabled a humanoid to learn 22 novel behaviors from only synthetic video, reaching 43.2% success on new behaviors and 28.5% in unseen environments (vs 0% baseline).

By June 2026 NVIDIA had released Isaac GR00T N1.7 (open VLA), and announced the Isaac GR00T Reference Humanoid Robot built on Jetson AGX Thor (Blackwell GPU, 2,070 FP4 TFLOPS, 128GB) with a Unitree H2 Plus body and Sharpa hands, shipping Oct 2026.

Wayve GAIA-1 (arXiv 2309.17080, Sep 2023) was a 9-billion-parameter generative world model trained on ~4,700 hours of UK driving, casting world modeling as next-token prediction over discrete video/text/action tokens.

Wayve GAIA-2 (arXiv 2503.20523, Mar 26 2025) is an 8.4B-parameter space-time factorized latent-diffusion transformer (22 layers, hidden dim 4096) generating 5 coherent camera views at 448x960; its video tokenizer uses 32x spatial / 8x temporal compression (64-channel latent), trained on ~25 million 2-second sequences (~139,000 hours) across UK/US/Germany.

Wayve GAIA-3 (launched Dec 2 2025) is a 15-billion-parameter model (double GAIA-2) trained on 10x more data, shifting world models from visual synthesis to autonomy evaluation with three new modes (safety-critical scenario generation, embodiment transfer, controlled visual diversity); early testing reported a 5x reduction in synthetic-test rejection rates.

NVIDIA Alpamayo-1 (announced CES Jan 2026) is a 10-billion-parameter chain-of-thought reasoning vision-language-action model for autonomous vehicles, released open-source with the Physical AI AV dataset (1,727 hours, 25 countries, 2,500+ cities, camera+LiDAR+radar) and the AlpaSim simulator; adopters include JLR, Lucid, and Uber.

Waabi's Copilot4D is a self-supervised LiDAR world model that tokenizes continuous LiDAR into discrete tokens and forecasts via discrete diffusion 5-10 seconds into the future; an advanced version runs on Waabi's autonomous trucks delivering commercial loads with Uber Freight in Texas.

Tesla generates real-time 3D drivable environments from its 8-vehicle cameras to train FSD (v13-v14), letting engineers inject rare events (running pedestrians, fog, sudden lane changes); Tesla launched a geofenced robotaxi service in Austin on June 22 2025.

Vista (NeurIPS 2024, arXiv 2405.17398) is a generalizable driving world model predicting futures at 10 Hz and 576x1024 resolution with multi-modal action control (steering, speed, trajectory, goal point), surpassing the best prior driving world model by 55% in FID and 27% in FVD.

Meta's V-JEPA 2 (arXiv 2506.09985, Jun 2025) is a 1B+-parameter ViT-g video encoder pretrained on 1M+ hours of video; the action-conditioned V-JEPA 2-AC (~300M) was post-trained on under 62 hours of unlabeled Droid robot video and deployed zero-shot on Franka arms via MPC/CEM planning, achieving 65-80% pick-and-place success at 16 seconds per action (vs Cosmos at ~4 minutes per action).

DreamerV3 (Nature 2025, 'Mastering diverse control tasks through world models') is a single-configuration model-based RL algorithm that outperforms specialized methods across 150+ tasks and is the first to collect diamonds in Minecraft from scratch without human data or curricula.

TD-MPC2 (arXiv 2310.16828) performs latent-space trajectory optimization in a decoder-free implicit world model, scaling a single 317M-parameter agent to 80 tasks across embodiments and beating DreamerV3 and SAC across 104 continuous-control tasks with one hyperparameter set.

DINO-WM (arXiv 2411.04983, NYU/Meta-FAIR incl. LeCun & Pinto, Nov 2024) builds a decoder-free world model on frozen DINOv2 patch features and plans zero-shot via CEM on latent MSE, achieving 0.90 success on Push-T (vs DreamerV3 0.04, TD-MPC2 0.00) and best chamfer distance on Rope/Granular manipulation.

Meta's Navigation World Model (NWM, arXiv 2412.03572, FAIR/NYU/Berkeley incl. LeCun, CVPR 2025) is a 1B-parameter Conditional Diffusion Transformer (CDiT) trained on egocentric human+robot video that plans navigation by simulating and ranking candidate trajectories and can imagine routes in unseen environments from a single image.

Early industry adopters of NVIDIA Cosmos for generating physical-AI training data include 1X, Agility Robotics, Figure AI, Foretellix, Skild AI, and Uber, with the photorealistic data used to post-train policy models such as GR00T N1 for sim-to-real transfer.

openQuestions: Generative video world models (Cosmos, GAIA) are photorealistic and scalable but physically imperfect and far too slow for real-time control (Cosmos ~4 min/action vs V-JEPA 2-AC 16s); whether latent/JEPA-style models can reach both fidelity and real-time speed remains open.

Quantitative, apples-to-apples sim2real transfer evidence is still thin: most papers report that synthetic world-model data 'helps' policies, but rigorous measures of how much real-robot performance is attributable to world-model data vs other factors are scarce.

Driving world models still lack standardized closed-loop evaluation; GAIA-3 and AlpaSim explicitly target this, but there is no agreed benchmark equating generated-scenario rejection rates to real-world safety outcomes.

It is unclear whether next-token / diffusion video prediction actually learns physical causality and 3D geometry, or merely surface statistics — Cosmos-Reason1 benchmarks (~52-67% on physics commonsense) suggest large remaining gaps.
Whether a single cross-embodiment world model (e.g. Cosmos/GR00T) truly transfers across robot bodies, or whether per-embodiment fine-tuning and adapters remain necessary, is not yet resolved.

Tesla's and other AV makers' 'world model' claims (real-time 3D world generation for FSD v14) are largely marketing/keynote statements without published architectures, parameter counts, or peer-reviewed results, making independent assessment impossible.

The compute and data economics are extreme (Cosmos: ~20M video hours, 10k H100s for 3 months), raising open questions about who can train frontier world models and how much the open-weight releases (NVIDIA Open Model License) actually democratize this.

title: Evaluation, benchmarks & metrics
summary: World-model evaluation splits into two largely disjoint traditions. (1) Control/RL agents (Dreamer line) are judged by downstream return and sample efficiency, not prediction error. DreamerV3 (arXiv:2301.04104) uses fixed hyperparameters across 150+ tasks/8 domains, reports human-/gamer-normalized scores (Atari-100k median 49%, vs IRIS 29%, EfficientZero 109%), and is the first agent to mine Minecraft diamonds from scratch (24/40 seeds). Its actor-critic trains entirely in latent imagination rollouts. (2) Generative video world simulators are judged on visual fidelity and physical plausibility. The dominant distributional metric, Frechet Video Distance (FVD), is heavily criticized: I3D features are non-Gaussian, insensitive to temporal distortion, biased toward per-frame appearance, and need thousands of clips to converge (arXiv:2410.05203). This drove physics-focused benchmarks. Physion/Physion++ (object-contact prediction; latent-property inference) show object-centric/GNN models beat pixel models but all fall far below humans. The 2025-26 wave is damning: PhyGenBench (arXiv:2410.05363) finds best model Gen-3 scores only 0.51 PCA across 160 prompts/27 laws; Google-DeepMind/INSAIT Physics-IQ (arXiv:2501.09038) shows best model VideoPoet at 29.5% vs a 100% physical-variance ceiling, Sora last at 10.0%, and crucially visual realism is uncorrelated with physics (Pearson r=-0.46, n.s.). ByteDance PhyWorld (arXiv:2411.02385, ICML 2025) shows video models do perfect in-distribution but fail OOD (velocity error 0.012 to 0.427, no improvement with 100x more data), generalize case-based (nearest-example mimicry) with attribute priority color >> size >> velocity >> shape. WorldModelBench (arXiv:2502.20694) crowdsources 67K labels, scores instruction-following/common-sense/physical-adherence (5 binary laws), trains a 2B judger (+8.6% over GPT-4o); dominant violations are mass-conservation (12%), interpenetration (11%), gravity (7%). VBench-2.0 (arXiv:2503.21755) adds intrinsic faithfulness (physics/commonsense), exposing fake motion. Long-horizon rollout drift (compounding error, energy drift, train-on-GT/test-on-self distribution shift) is the central failure mode (Orbis arXiv:2507.13162). The 2026 frontier critique (World-in-World arXiv:2510.18135) argues open-loop visual quality does NOT predict closed-loop task success; controllability matters more, pushing toward closed-loop, action-conditioned, rank-consistency evaluation.

keyClaims.claim: DreamerV3 is evaluated by downstream return via human-/gamer-normalized scores across 150+ tasks in 8 domains using a single fixed hyperparameter set; it scores 49% human-normalized median on Atari-100k (vs IRIS 29%, EfficientZero 109% with extra search), and its actor-critic is trained entirely in latent imagination rollouts, emphasizing sample efficiency over pixel accuracy.

DreamerV3 was the first algorithm to collect diamonds in Minecraft from scratch without human data or curricula (24 of 40 seeds succeeded over 100M steps), and performance/data-efficiency improve monotonically with model size from 8M to 200M parameters without hyperparameter changes, a sample-efficiency-and-scaling evaluation rather than prediction-error.

On Atari-100k, HarmonyDream (built on DreamerV3) reaches 136.5% mean human performance, the SOTA among methods without lookahead search; the standard sample-efficiency benchmark fixes the agent to 100k environment steps (~2 hours of gameplay).

Frechet Video Distance (FVD), the dominant distributional metric for video world models, has three core flaws: non-Gaussian I3D feature space, I3D insensitivity to temporal distortions (biasing it toward per-frame appearance over motion/temporal coherence), and the need for thousands of clips to converge; FID-VID/FVD measure appearance match but not whether motion matches the target. Alternatives proposed include JEDi and Frechet Video Motion Distance (FVMD).

Physion evaluates physical prediction via the Object Contact Prediction (OCP) task across 8 scenario types (collisions, support/containment, rolling, sliding, projectile, soft-body/cloth); object-centric vision models outperform non-object-centric ones, GNNs with direct physical-state access do best and most human-like, but all fall far short of human accuracy, identifying physical-representation extraction as the bottleneck.

Physion++ extends evaluation to online inference of latent physical properties (mass, friction, elasticity, deformability) across 9 scenarios with an inference period then a contact-prediction period; models trained with standard regimes do not spontaneously infer latent properties, there remains a huge gap to humans, and model predictions correlate poorly with human predictions.

Google-DeepMind/INSAIT Physics-IQ (396 real high-quality videos; 5 categories: solid mechanics, fluid dynamics, optics, thermodynamics, magnetism) scores models 0-100% relative to a physical-variance ceiling (100); the best model VideoPoet-multiframe reaches only 29.5%, Runway Gen-3 22.8%, Stable Video Diffusion 14.8%, Pika 1.0 13.0%, and Sora last at 10.0%, i.e. 70+ points below ceiling.

Physics-IQ demonstrates that visual realism is uncorrelated with physical understanding: Sora achieved the best multimodal-LLM realism score (55.6%, least distinguishable from real) yet ranked worst on Physics-IQ (10.0%); across all models Pearson r = -0.46 (p=.249, not significant), direct evidence that perceptual-quality metrics do not measure world-modeling.

The Physics-IQ score aggregates four sub-metrics: Spatial IoU, Spatiotemporal IoU, Weighted Spatial IoU (higher-is-better) and MSE (lower-is-better) measured against the action region of real continuation videos; the physical-variance reference reaches Spatial IoU 0.678 / Spatiotemporal 0.535 / Weighted 0.577 / MSE 0.002, while the best model (VideoPoet) reaches only 0.204 / 0.164 / 0.137 / 0.010.

ByteDance PhyWorld (How Far is Video Generation from World Model, ICML 2025) uses a Box2D 2D classical-mechanics testbed (uniform motion, elastic collision, parabola) and finds near-perfect in-distribution generalization (uniform-motion velocity error ~0.012) but order-of-magnitude-worse out-of-distribution error (0.427), with NO improvement scaling data from 30K to 3M videos, showing scaling alone cannot make video models discover physical laws.

PhyWorld shows video models generalize case-based (mimicking the nearest training example rather than abstracting rules) and resolve ambiguity via a fixed visual-attribute priority color >> size >> velocity >> shape (e.g., a blue ball is rendered into a blue square to match a blue-square training case); combinatorial diversity helps more than volume, scaling templates 6 to 60 cut the physically-implausible abnormal rate from 67% to 10%.

PhyGenBench evaluates physical commonsense across 27 laws / 160 prompts in 4 domains (mechanics, optics, thermal, material) using the hierarchical PhyGenEval pipeline (key-phenomena detection, physics-order/causality verification, overall naturalness, via VLMs with GPT-4o-generated questions; human correlation Spearman 0.81); best model Gen-3 reaches only 0.51 Physical Commonsense Alignment (PCA), with Kling 0.49, CogVideoX-5B 0.45, Pika 0.44, Lavie 0.36, concluding T2V models are far from world simulators and scaling/prompt-engineering are insufficient.

WorldModelBench judges video generators on three axes: Instruction Following (0-3), Common Sense (temporal consistency + aesthetics), and Physical Adherence (5 binary laws: Newton first law/inertia, solid-mechanics deformation, fluid mechanics, impenetrability, gravity), across 7 application domains, 56 subdomains, 350 prompts, with 67K crowd-sourced human labels and 14 frontier models; dominant violation categories are mass-conservation (12%), object interpenetration (11%), and gravity violation (7%).

WorldModelBench trains a 2B-parameter multimodal judger aligned to its human labels that predicts world-modeling violations with 8.6% higher average accuracy than GPT-4o; using this judger as a reward to fine-tune OpenSora-v1.2 raised its aggregate WorldModelBench score from 6.17 to 6.56 with fewer gravity violations and reduced flicker, so the benchmark doubles as a trainable reward signal.

On the WorldModelBench leaderboard, closed models lead: KLING ~8.82/10 (61% instruction execution), Minimax 8.59, Mochi-official 8.37, open Mochi 7.62, OpenSoraPlan-T2V 7.61, illustrating a gap between closed frontier and open models on combined instruction/commonsense/physics scoring.

VBench-2.0 introduces intrinsic faithfulness (5 dimensions, 18 sub-abilities) beyond VBench-1.0 superficial faithfulness, adding Physics (State Change: Mechanics/Thermotics/Material; Geometry: Multi-View Consistency) and Commonsense (Motion Rationality, Instance Preservation); evaluation uses VLM multi-question answering plus specialized tools (ArcFace identity, YOLO-World counting, RAFT optical flow, SIFT/FLANN/RANSAC geometry).

VBench-2.0 exposes a failure mode termed fake motions: visually plausible but causally incorrect dynamics such as eating without food being consumed or walking without forward progress; frontier models are weak on dynamic attribute change (HunyuanVideo 22.71%) and complex multi-scene plots (~10-20%), even while scoring 86-88% on Human Fidelity.

The central quantitative failure mode of autoregressive/long-horizon world models is compounding error: models trained on ground-truth context but tested on self-generated context (train-test mismatch) drift off the data manifold, producing energy drift, unstable acceleration and physically inconsistent geometry; driving world models (Orbis) measure this with FVD/FID degradation, noting naive rollouts diverge into artifacts beyond ~8-12 steps.

In model-based RL, a documented failure mode is world-model exploitation / hallucinated reward: when uncertainty is unconstrained, policies inflate imagined returns by exploiting model inaccuracies, appearing optimal in imagination while violating real dynamics, manifesting on hardware as unstable walking, collisions, or locomotion breakdown despite high imagined return (objective/value mismatch from rollout drift).

World-in-World (arXiv:2510.18135) is the first open platform benchmarking world models in a closed-loop action-environment setting across four environments with task success as the primary metric; its headline finding is that visual quality alone does not guarantee task success (controllability matters more), that post-training with action-observation data beats upgrading pretrained video generators, and that more inference-time compute substantially improves closed-loop performance.

The 2026 evaluation consensus is shifting from open-loop perceptual metrics to closed-loop functional metrics: action-conditioned consistency, rank-consistency (does the model correctly rank outcomes of different actions), and downstream decision reliability, recognizing that a blurry-but-causally-correct prediction can beat a photorealistic-but-physically-inconsistent one; most existing benchmarks still use open-loop protocols, leaving embodied utility unresolved.

A new wave of embodied/robotic world-model benchmarks evaluates functional utility rather than pixels: EWMBench (task-conditioned video synthesis of agent-environment interaction), RoboWM-Bench (converts predicted manipulation behaviors into executable actions and measures simulated task completion), and WorldArena (unified perception + functional-utility, controllability, action-conditioning, closed-loop), reflecting criticism that prior benchmarks over-target text-conditioned video and under-cover action-conditioned robot-centric models.

keyPapers.oneLine: Foundational physical-prediction benchmark using Object Contact Prediction across 8 dynamics scenarios; object-centric/GNN models beat pixel models but all trail humans.

keyPapers.oneLine: Extends Physion to latent-property inference (mass, friction, elasticity, deformability); all models far below humans and poorly correlated with human judgments.

keyPapers.oneLine: Catalogs FVD flaws (non-Gaussian I3D features, temporal-distortion insensitivity, huge sample-size needs) motivating better distributional metrics like JEDi.

keyPapers.oneLine: 396 real-video physics benchmark (Google-DeepMind/INSAIT); best model 29.5% vs 100% ceiling, Sora 10%, and visual realism uncorrelated with physics (r=-0.46).

keyPapers.oneLine: Box2D study (ICML 2025): perfect in-distribution but failing OOD (no improvement with 100x data); generalization is case-based with attribute priority color>>size>>velocity>>shape.

keyPapers.oneLine: 67K-human-label benchmark over 7 domains scoring instruction-following/common-sense/physical-adherence (5 laws); trains a 2B judger (+8.6% over GPT-4o) usable as a fine-tuning reward.

keyPapers.oneLine: First closed-loop world-model benchmark; shows visual quality does not predict task success (controllability matters more), arguing for embodied closed-loop evaluation.

keyPapers.title: World Model for Robot Learning: A Comprehensive Survey
keyPapers.oneLine: 2026 survey synthesizing the shift from perceptual metrics to action-conditioned consistency, rank-consistency, and downstream-utility evaluation for robotic world models.

openQuestions: There is no single accepted metric that bridges open-loop prediction quality and closed-loop task success; benchmarks like World-in-World show they can diverge, but a cheap predictive surrogate that forecasts downstream control performance remains unestablished.
FVD is widely used yet broadly discredited (content bias, sample-size sensitivity); the field lacks consensus on a replacement, with JEDi, FVMD, and VLM-judge scores all competing and none dominant.

Physics benchmarks disagree on whether physical understanding is emerging at all: PhyWorld and Physics-IQ argue scaling alone fails and generalization is case-based/memorized, while some results (fluid dynamics outperforming solid mechanics; combinatorial diversity cutting abnormal rates) suggest partial acquisition is possible, so conditions for genuine OOD physical generalization are unresolved.

VLM/MLLM-based judger evaluation (WorldModelBench 2B judger, PhyGenEval, VBench-2.0 QA) inherits the judging model limitations and may be gameable when used as a training reward; robustness of these automated judges to reward-hacking and OOD generations is open.

Standardized long-horizon drift metrics are immature: papers report energy drift, abnormal rates, and FVD-vs-horizon curves ad hoc, with no agreed protocol for horizon length, error-accumulation quantification, or train-on-GT/test-on-self gap measurement across domains.

Action-conditioned/embodied benchmarks (EWMBench, RoboWM-Bench, WorldArena, World-in-World) are very new (2025-2026) and not yet consolidated; whether the community converges on a shared closed-loop suite analogous to Atari-100k/DMC for control remains to be seen.

title: Limitations, critiques & debates
summary: As of mid-2026, the "world models" field is split by a foundational debate over whether generative video models constitute genuine world models. The flashpoint is Yann LeCun, who in Nov 2025 announced his departure from Meta to found AMI Labs (Advanced Machine Intelligence Labs; raised $1.03B at $3.5B pre-money valuation in March 2026), declaring LLMs "a dead end" for superintelligence and that "generation is very different from causal prediction from a world model." His JEPA/V-JEPA thesis: pixel reconstruction is wasteful, produces "blurry averages," and models should predict in abstract latent space. The opposing "generative" camp—OpenAI Sora/Sora 2, Google DeepMind Genie 3/Veo, Wayve, NVIDIA Cosmos—argues realistic video implies physical understanding. Eric Xing counter-critiques LeCun: latent prediction without a generative decoder "is prone to losing contact with reality" (debated live at Spring School AI For Impact, March 2026). A July 2025 arXiv paper "Critiques of World Models" (2507.05169) formally challenges LeCun's five claims, proving (Proposition 1) JEPA latent losses can collapse to constants and (Theorem 2) latent losses are upper-bounded surrogates for generative ones. Empirically, Kang et al. (ByteDance/Tsinghua/Technion, "How Far is Video Generation from World Model," 2411.02385) showed video diffusion fails OOD generalization (OOD error ~10x ID error, no improvement with scale), exhibiting "case-based" mimicry with attribute hierarchy color>>size>>velocity>>shape. Gary Marcus argues Sora knows "pixels, not objects," fails object permanence, and that "the John Locke hypothesis" (learning physics from sense data alone) is failing. Rich Sutton (Sep 2025 Dwarkesh) calls LLMs "mimicry engines" lacking true world models. Genuinely unsolved as of 2026: long-horizon drift/error accumulation, 3D/spatial memory consistency beyond ~1 minute, prohibitive compute for real-time long-context generation, true causal/counterfactual reasoning, and the realism-vs-utility gap (visual quality doesn't predict task success per World-in-World/WorldModelBench).

keyClaims.claim: Yann LeCun left Meta in Nov 2025 (confirmed Nov 19, 2025) after ~10 years to found AMI Labs (Advanced Machine Intelligence Labs), focused on JEPA/V-JEPA world-model architectures; he stated 'LLMs basically are a dead end when it comes to superintelligence' and AMI raised $1.03B at a $3.5B pre-money valuation in March 2026.

LeCun's central critique: 'the generation of mostly realistic-looking videos from prompts does not indicate that a system understands the physical world. Generation is very different from causal prediction from a world model.' He argues pixel reconstruction is wasteful because most detail is unpredictable, causing blurry outputs; the fix is predicting in abstract latent representation space (JEPA), regularized against collapse with methods like VICReg.

The July 2025 arXiv paper 'Critiques of World Models' (2507.05169) systematically challenges LeCun's five claims (data priority, continuous representation, JEPA architecture, latent-space objective, MPC-over-RL). It argues JEPA is 'fundamentally autoregressive and generative,' proves via Proposition 1 that latent reconstruction losses can collapse (mapping all observations to constants, learning no dynamics), and via Theorem 2 that latent losses are upper-bounded surrogates for generative losses. It proposes a PAN (Physical, Agentic, Nested) / Generative Latent Prediction alternative.

Eric Xing counters LeCun: an abstract latent-prediction world model without a generative decoder/validator 'is prone to losing contact with reality.' The LeCun–Xing dispute (debated at Spring School AI For Impact, March 2026) turns on whether to attach a decoder and on what counts as predictive success.

Kang & Yue et al. (ByteDance Research, Tsinghua, Technion; 'How Far is Video Generation from World Model: A Physical Law Perspective,' arXiv 2411.02385) trained diffusion video models (22M–310M params, 30K–3M examples) on 2D classical-mechanics videos. Finding: near-perfect in-distribution generalization but out-of-distribution error ~an order of magnitude higher with minimal improvement from scaling (uniform-motion OOD error stayed ~0.35–0.43 regardless of data size). Models do 'case-based' generalization (mimic nearest training example), prioritizing attributes color>>size>>velocity>>shape. Conclusion: 'scaling alone is insufficient for video generation models to uncover fundamental physical laws.'

Gary Marcus argues Sora has not learned physics: 'The laws of physics are about objects, not pixels; Sora knows only about pixels and image spaces, not objects' and 'Whenever there is a conflict between physics and image sequence prediction, image sequence prediction wins.' He documents object-permanence failures (people/animals winking in and out of existence), levitating chairs, balls passing through rims, and six-fingered humans, concluding the 'John Locke hypothesis' (learning physics from sense data alone) is failing and 'more data won't solve' it.

Rich Sutton (Dwarkesh Podcast, Sep 26, 2025) argues LLMs 'don't truly have world models; they just mimic entities that do—people,' calls them 'mimicry engines,' and says 'A real world model predicts what happens in the world, not just what a person is likely to say.' He frames intelligence as grounded in goals, action, and a stream of experience (RL), noting next-token prediction 'doesn't change the world.'

Long-horizon drift / error accumulation is a defining unsolved failure mode: autoregressive generation gradually drifts from earlier scene states causing identity drift, temporal wobble, object warping, color over-saturation, and even collapse to static output. 2026 papers (MagicWorld, WorldWeaver, LIVE, RELIC) propose flow-guided motion constraints, depth cues (more drift-resistant than RGB), cycle-consistency, and compressed memory as partial fixes.

3D/spatial memory consistency is unsolved beyond short horizons: Genie 3 reaches 'emergent multi-minute consistency' but only retains coherent object state for about a minute. The core tension is that explicit 3D generators (NeRF/Gaussian Splatting, e.g. World Labs) give stable navigation but require explicit spatial modeling, while implicit frame-by-frame generators are flexible but brittle, losing context and hallucinating objects over extended rollouts. RELIC notes most prior models train on only 5-second contexts; it extends to ~20s (317 frames) but 'struggles to generate extremely long videos—on the scale of minutes.'

Compute cost is a hard constraint on interactive/long-horizon world models: MAGI-1-4.5B-distill needs ~32GB memory and ~50 minutes inference to generate a 10-second 720x720 video with full KV cache on an A800. Real-time generation is achievable only at limited resolution/length (e.g. an 8B model at 24fps, 736x416 on a single H100, or 1280x720 on 8xH100 up to a minute). Long-context processing cost is described as 'prohibitively high,' forcing short temporal windows that discard prior information.

Closed-loop evaluation shows realism does not predict usefulness: World-in-World (arXiv 2510.18135, Oct 2025) finds 'world models with strong visual scores do not necessarily bring high success rates,' that controllability matters more than visual quality, and that scaling action-observation post-training and inference-time compute help more than upgrading the pretrained video generator. WorldModelBench (arXiv 2502.20694, NeurIPS 2025) evaluated 14 frontier models with 67K human labels on instruction-following and physics-adherence, detecting violations like irregular object-size changes breaching mass conservation that prior quality-only benchmarks missed.

Even non-generative / latent world models show large intuitive-physics gaps: on IntPhys 2 and similar benchmarks humans score ~85–95% while top models including V-JEPA 2 perform near chance (~50%) in complex scenes. The opinion paper 'Learning Intuitive Physics May Require More than Visual Data' (Su, Legris, Gureckis, Ren; arXiv 2512.06232, Dec 2025) finds training on developmentally realistic video (e.g. SAYCam, ~0.01% of SOTA data volume) does not significantly improve IntPhys2 performance, concluding human-like physics may require interaction/multimodal signals beyond passive video.

True causal/counterfactual reasoning remains a recognized gap: critics argue Sora 'cannot respond to LeCun's causal law' (e.g. 'how will the ball fly if I kick it')—it remembers probabilities rather than understanding mechanics. Research finds LLMs' apparent causal competence may reflect 'semantic pattern recombination rather than structure-sensitive causal reasoning,' motivating frameworks like Causal World Model Induction (CWMI) with a Causal Physics Module and Causal Intervention Loss.

The field lacks an agreed definition of 'world model,' splitting between 'understanding the world' (Ha & Schmidhuber's abstraction view) and 'predicting the future' (LeCun's decision-oriented view); definitional shakiness has led some researchers to explicitly reject the 'world model' label, and critics call the most-hyped current use case 'AI video slop.'

openQuestions: Long-horizon temporal/spatial consistency beyond ~1 minute remains unsolved; autoregressive error accumulation (drift, warping, identity loss, collapse to static frames) has only partial mitigations (cycle-consistency, depth cues, flow constraints, compressed memory).

Whether physical/causal understanding can emerge from passive visual data alone (the 'John Locke hypothesis') or whether it fundamentally requires embodied interaction, action-conditioning, or multimodal grounding is empirically contested and unresolved.

The architectural question: does the JEPA latent-prediction approach (LeCun/AMI) actually beat generative pixel/token prediction, or does latent prediction 'lose contact with reality' without a decoder (Xing) and risk representation collapse (Critiques of World Models)? Neither side has decisive evidence as of mid-2026.

Compute economics: real-time, high-resolution, minute-plus interactive world models remain prohibitively expensive (quadratic context cost); it is unclear whether efficiency tricks (sparse attention, cache compression, distillation) can close the gap to genuinely useful long-horizon simulation.

Evaluation: the field has not converged on metrics; closed-loop task-success benchmarks (World-in-World, WorldModelBench) show realism is a weak proxy for utility, but standardized, decision-relevant evaluation of 'world-modeling' capability is still immature.

Definitional: there is no agreed definition of what makes something a 'world model' (understanding vs prediction, with vs without a generative decoder, internal vs explicit state), fueling the 'is it really a world model / hype' debate and prompting some labs to drop the term.

Out-of-distribution and combinatorial generalization of learned physics is weak; whether scale plus better data/objectives can move models from 'case-based' memorization to abstracting general physical laws is open and currently trending negative for pure scaling.

verifiedClaims.evidence:
Nearly every specific, falsifiable element of the claim is confirmed by primary/high-quality sources, INCLUDING the three cited URLs. The single inaccuracy is the tenure figure.

CONFIRMED:
1) Departure confirmed Nov 19, 2025: CNBC (cnbc.com/2025/11/19) and Bloomberg both report LeCun announced his exit "on Wednesday (November 19)" 2025 via a memo/LinkedIn post. (Nov 19, 2025 was indeed a Wednesday — internally consistent. Fortune's "Nov 18" appears to be a minor error; the LinkedIn/memo announcement was Nov 19.)
2) Company name: the-decoder, Fortune, and TechCrunch all confirm "Advanced Machine Intelligence (AMI) Labs."
3) JEPA/V-JEPA world models: the-decoder states the venture is "betting on an alternative to LLMs built around V-JEPA"; TechCrunch references JEPA (Joint Embedding Predictive Architecture). Confirmed.
4) Quote: the cited the-decoder article reproduces verbatim "LLMs basically are a dead end when it comes to superintelligence" (originally from an FT interview). Confirmed.
5) Funding: TechCrunch (Mar 9, 2026) and Bloomberg (Mar 10, 2026) both confirm AMI Labs raised $1.03 billion at a $3.5 billion pre-money valuation, the largest prelaunch/seed raise in European history. Confirmed (announced March 9–10, 2026).

THE ONE ERROR — tenure: The claim says "~10 years." LeCun joined Facebook/Meta as founding director of FAIR in December 2013 and departed end of 2025 = approximately 12 years. Fortune explicitly says "12 years" (5 as founding director + 7 as chief AI scientist); the-decoder says "more than a decade"; a search summary also says 12 years. "~10 years" understates the actual ~12-year tenure.

Net: all load-bearing facts (date, name, architecture, quote, funding amount, valuation, timing) are accurate; only the tenure figure is mildly wrong, so the claim is partially-supported (strongly leaning true).

title: Frontier 2025-2026 & industry landscape
summary: 2025-2026 was the inflection year when "world models" went from research concept to a contested product category and a major funding magnet. The defining axis is real-time interactivity: DeepMind's Genie 3 (Aug 2025) generates navigable 720p/24fps worlds from text, consistent for "several minutes" with ~1-minute visual memory, supporting promptable world events; it was productized as "Project Genie" for Google AI Ultra subscribers (US) on Jan 29, 2026, and paired with the Gemini-powered SIMA 2 agent (Nov 2025) to create an agent-training loop. World Labs (Fei-Fei Li) shipped its first commercial product Marble (Nov 12, 2025), generating persistent 3D worlds exportable as Gaussian splats/meshes ($20-$95/mo tiers), plus research preview RTFM (Oct 2025), a single-H100 autoregressive diffusion world model. Runway launched GWM-1 (Dec 11, 2025), an autoregressive world model on Gen-4.5 in three variants (Worlds, Avatars, Robotics). Decart shipped Oasis 2.0 (1080p/30fps real-time video-to-video via MirageLSD). On the physical-AI side, NVIDIA's Cosmos evolved from CES 2025 launch to Cosmos 3 (GTC Taipei, ~May 2026), an open mixture-of-transformers omnimodel (Super/Nano/Edge). Wayve advanced GAIA-2 (Mar 2025) to GAIA-3 (Dec 2, 2025), a 15B-parameter driving world model claiming 5x lower synthetic-test rejection. Meta's V-JEPA 2 (Jun 2025) is the leading non-generative (joint-embedding) world model, 1.2B params, enabling zero-shot robot pick-and-place. Tesla disclosed FSD v14's generative world model / neural closed-loop sim (ICCV 2025). OpenAI's Sora 2 (Sep/Oct 2025) advanced physics realism and world-state persistence. Funding exploded: Decart raised $300M at $4B (May 2026, NVIDIA-backed); World Labs raised ~$1B; and Yann LeCun left Meta (Nov 2025) to found Paris-based AMI Labs, raising a $1.03B seed (Mar 2026) explicitly to build JEPA-based world models as a contrarian bet against LLMs. Near-term direction: longer-horizon consistency, action-conditioning, omni-models (text+vision+action), physical-reasoning benchmarks, and embodied-agent/robotics training.

keyClaims.claim: DeepMind unveiled Genie 3 in August 2025 as a real-time interactive general-purpose world model generating 720p worlds at 24 fps from text prompts, remaining largely consistent for several minutes with a visual memory horizon of up to ~1 minute; it supports 'promptable world events' (changing weather, adding objects/characters) and uses auto-regressive frame generation with long-range attention.

Genie 3 was productized as 'Project Genie,' an experimental prototype released January 29, 2026 to Google AI Ultra subscribers in the United States, generating explorable worlds from text/image prompts.

DeepMind announced SIMA 2 in November 2025, a Gemini (2.5 Flash Lite)-powered generalist embodied agent that reasons in language, self-improves via trial-and-error with Gemini feedback, and was integrated with Genie 3 so agents can train across unlimited generated environments.

World Labs (founded by Fei-Fei Li, CEO; Justin Johnson co-founder) launched Marble on November 12, 2025 as its first commercial product, generating persistent downloadable 3D worlds from text/image/video/panorama/3D-layout inputs, exportable as Gaussian splats, meshes, or video, across free/$20/$35/$95-per-month tiers, with a 'Chisel' 3D editor and Vision Pro/Quest 3 support.

World Labs released RTFM (Real-Time Frame Model) as a research preview in October 2025: an autoregressive diffusion transformer with spatial memory that renders persistent, 3D-consistent worlds at interactive frame rates on a single NVIDIA H100 GPU, without explicit 3D geometry.

World Labs raised approximately $1 billion to advance spatial intelligence (following $230M when it emerged from stealth in September 2024), positioning spatial intelligence as the defining AI challenge of the next decade.

Runway launched GWM-1 on December 11, 2025, its first General World Model: an autoregressive model built on Gen-4.5 generating frame-by-frame in real time at 720p up to 2 minutes, controllable via camera pose/events/robot pose/speech, in three variants (GWM Worlds, GWM Avatars, GWM Robotics). Runway argues 'language models alone won't solve robotics, disease, scientific discovery' and that world models are 'the most clear path to general-purpose simulation.'

Yann LeCun left Meta in November 2025 (after 12 years as chief AI scientist) to found Paris-based AMI Labs (Advanced Machine Intelligence), raising a $1.03B seed in March 2026 at a $3.5B pre-money valuation — the largest prelaunch AI funding in European history — to build JEPA-based world models as a contrarian bet against LLMs; LeCun is executive chairman with Alexandre LeBrun (Nabla) as CEO, and Meta retains a research partnership.

Tesla VP of Autonomous Driving Ashok Eluswamy disclosed at ICCV 2025 that FSD v14 uses a generative world model treating the environment as a 4D simulation, with a multimodal system (video, navigation, vehicle status, sound inputs; outputs include 3D occupancy, 3D Gaussian reconstruction, language decisions, control), trained via a neural-network closed-loop simulation comparing against human ground truth. FSD v14 began rolling out October 2025.

OpenAI's Sora 2 (released ~late September/October 2025) advanced physics realism and world-state persistence: it models rebounds, momentum and buoyancy, can persist scene state/character continuity/blocking across multiple shots, generates synchronized audio/speech/sound effects, and introduced 'cameos' inserting a real person (from a reference video) into generated scenes. openQuestions: Generative (pixel-predictive, e.g., Genie 3, Cosmos, Sora 2) vs non-generative joint-embedding (JEPA / AMI Labs) world models: which paradigm wins for embodied planning, and does LeCun's $1.03B bet against LLMs/generative video pay off?
Long-horizon consistency remains the central unsolved problem: Genie 3 holds ~1 minute of memory and 'several minutes' of coherence — when do world models reach hours of persistent, drift-free state?
Do today's video world models actually learn physics, or pattern-match appearances? Benchmarks like IntPhys 2 show models near chance vs 85-95% human, leaving real physical understanding unproven.
Will real-time world models become viable training environments that measurably improve real robot/AV policies (sim-to-real transfer), beyond synthetic-data augmentation?
Business-model viability: is there durable demand/willingness-to-pay for consumer 3D-world generation (Marble, Project Genie) versus B2B physical-AI/AV simulation (Cosmos, GAIA, Decart Oasis)?
Compute and latency: can persistent, high-resolution interactive worlds run economically at scale, or do single-H100/sub-35ms claims break down for multi-user persistent environments?
Consolidation vs fragmentation: with NVIDIA backing Decart and supplying Cosmos, plus DeepMind/Meta/OpenAI in-house efforts, do independent world-model startups get acquired or squeezed?

Evaluation standards: the field still lacks agreed benchmarks for interactive long-horizon world fidelity, controllability, and physical alignment — which benchmark (WorldPrediction, IntPhys 2, etc.) becomes canonical?

verifiedClaims.claim: DeepMind unveiled Genie 3 in August 2025 as a real-time interactive general-purpose world model generating 720p worlds at 24 fps from text prompts, largely consistent for several minutes with a visual memory horizon of ~1 minute; supports promptable world events (weather, objects/characters) and uses auto-regressive frame generation with long-range attention.
verifiedClaims.evidence:
Every factual element of the claim is confirmed by the primary source (DeepMind's official Genie 3 blog) and corroborated by the TechCrunch article and other independent reporting.

ANNOUNCEMENT DATE: Confirmed Aug 5, 2025. Both the DeepMind blog and TechCrunch (URL dated 2025/08/05) carry this date.

720p @ 24 fps from text: DeepMind blog states Genie 3 generates "dynamic worlds that you can navigate in real time at 24 frames per second" at "720p" resolution from a text prompt. TechCrunch independently: "720p resolution at 24 frames per second."

CONSISTENCY FOR SEVERAL MINUTES + ~1 MIN VISUAL MEMORY: DeepMind blog: "Genie 3 environments remain largely consistent for several minutes, with visual memory extending as far back as one minute ago." Matches the claim's "largely consistent for several minutes" and "visual memory horizon of up to ~1 minute" verbatim in substance.

PROMPTABLE WORLD EVENTS (weather, objects/characters): DeepMind blog describes the ability to "change the generated world, like altering weather conditions or introducing new objects and characters." TechCrunch confirms "promptable world events, or the ability to use a prompt to change the generated world." Confirmed.

AUTO-REGRESSIVE FRAME GENERATION: DeepMind blog: "During the auto-regressive generation of each frame, the model has to take into account the previously generated trajectory that grows with time." TechCrunch: model "has to look back at what was generated before to decide what's going to happen next." Confirmed.

GENERAL-PURPOSE / FRONTIER FRAMING + AGI: DeepMind titled it "A new frontier for world models"; TechCrunch reports DeepMind positioned world models as "key on the path to AGI."

ONE MINOR NUANCE (not a refutation): The phrase "long-range attention" as a named architectural mechanism is NOT used in the official DeepMind blog, which instead calls consistency an "emergent capability" arising from the growing auto-regressive trajectory. The "long-range attention" / 11B-parameter transformer details appear only in third-party technical write-ups, not the cited primary sources. The substance (attending over long frame histories) is accurate, but the specific term is a third-party characterization rather than DeepMind's own wording. This does not contradict any claim.

Both claimed source URLs are real, live, and accurately quoted.
